articles.title: US limits visas for South African officials over alleged anti-white discrimination
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says South Africa has not addressed US concerns over racial inequality.

blocks.text: The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries.

The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers.
South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim.
"The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid ​out concerns," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the restrictions on Tuesday.
He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa."
Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions.

Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution."
But the South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land.
It said claims of a white genocide had been widely discredited and lacked reliable evidence.
South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that more white people have fallen victim to violent crime than other racial groups.
Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances.

The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court.

Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights.
The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures.
Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population.

In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States".
He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities.
"The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added.
He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law."
The South African government is yet to respond to the US restrictions.
The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations.

It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter."

South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House last May with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers.
But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited.

Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa.

The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests.

articles.title: Supreme Court presses Congress to enact anti-dynasty law
articles.summary: Supreme Court tells Congress to immediately pass a law defining and prohibiting political dynasties.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 2:12pm
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has urged Congress on Wednesday, September 16, to pass a law that defines and determines the scope of the prohibition against political dynasties “at the earliest opportunity.”

Supreme Court spokesperson Camille Ting announced that the high court has granted the consolidated petitions for certiorari and mandamus that challenged Congress’ failure to pass an anti-political dynasty law for almost four decades.

“By a majority vote, the Court likewise granted mandamus holding that Congress's failure to enact an anti-political dynasty law amounts to a refusal to perform a mandatory constitutional duty,” Ting said.
Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando cited Article 2, Section 26 of the Constitution in the ruling, stressing that the government has a “constitutional duty” to prohibit political dynasties.

Ting said the Supreme Court did not set a deadline for when the law must be enacted, as it also recognized that it cannot force Congress, as a co-equal branch of government, to perform a discretionary act.
A case may be filed before the high court in case Congress still fails to comply with the order, according to Ting.

“Well, we trust that the Congress will comply with the directive of the Supreme Court. But in case that does not happen, we will have to wait for the court's action and a case that may be filed before it,” Ting said.
Define dynasty
The Supreme Court stressed that the cited constitutional provision has made it clear that it is Congress’ mandate to ban political dynasties “as may be defined by law”.

“The phrase ‘as may be defined by law’ does not give Congress a choice whether to prohibit political dynasties. Rather, it gives Congress the authority to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition,” the Supreme Court said.
Ting said the court also determined that it reflected the framers' intentions of the 1987 Constitution.

“Records of the Constitutional Commission showed that the framers agreed to leave the definition of political dynasties to Congress after they could not agree on the specific family relationships and public positions that should be covered,” Ting said.
Grave abuse of discretion

While the Supreme Court also recognized the anti-political dynasty bills that had been filed in Congress, it also stressed that its prolonged failure to enact an appropriate one constituted a “grave use of discretion” and a violation of its mandate.

“The court found that 39 years is beyond a reasonable period to carry out the constitutional command. Congress has continued inaction, therefore, constitutes a continuing violation of its constitutional duty,” Ting said.
It also pointed out that political dynasties remain widespread and even extended into the party-list system.

“Despite changes in the composition of Congress over the years, no comprehensive anti-political dynasty law has been enacted, implying either a lack of interest, avoidance for convenience, or service of self-interest,” Ting added.
As of February 2026, 24 anti-political dynasty bills had been filed in Congress.
The Supreme Court stressed that while the Constitution did not set any deadline for Congress to define an anti-dynasty law, it does not allow the indefinite postponement of its enactment.

"The Congress of the Philippines must henceforth and with utmost urgency enact the appropriate anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity," the decision read, as quoted by Ting in a press briefing.

articles.title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year
articles.summary:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror

Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set…

blocks.text: Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled.

As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere.

Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.

According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely.
Though total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to their lowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply.

“Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year.

blocks.caption: Screenshot of a video filmed by JNIM fighters in Mansila, Burkina Faso, in 2024.

blocks.text: In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and their Russian auxiliaries with ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties.
Mali’s defence minister died in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed.

Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta in Mali three years ago.
Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries.
Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries.

blocks.caption: Three Russian mercenaries, on right, in northern Mali. Photograph: French Army/AP

blocks.text: In Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recent United Nations report based on intelligence supplied by member states.
Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies.

“In the Sahel, Islamic State and al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin.
The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years.

“In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.”
Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Chad and Nigeria, where they were targeted by US airstrikes last year.

The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing.

blocks.caption: A Somali police officer at the site of an al-Shabaab attack in Mogadishu in 2023. Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters

blocks.text: Though sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks.

At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes. Al-Qaida was also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds.
However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”.
Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022.

blocks.caption: There has been no declaration of who will succeed Ayman al-Zawahiri, seen here with Osama bin Laden in 2001, as al-Qaida leader since his death in 2022. Photograph: Daily Dawn/Reuters

blocks.text: Instead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-old Saif al-Adel, who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe.

The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US.
In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”.

But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa, the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%, from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled.

Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.

articles.title: News helicopter crashes in LA, killing 3
articles.summary: A helicopter belonging to an NBC news affiliate was covering a large traffic accident in the southern California city when it crashed. The cause is currently unclear.

image.caption: Dozens of firefighters responded to the crash in the San Fernando Valley, north of LA's downtownImage: Ethan Swope/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A news helicopter in Los Angeles crashed and burst into flames while covering a deadly bus accident on Tuesday evening.
At least three people were reported killed and a fourth was injured.
The helicopter crashed near a storage building in the Chatsworth neighborhood, northwest of downtown Los Angeles.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said at least one person was killed in the parking lot next to the building, adding it was currently unclear if the other two victims were on the ground or inside the aircraft. He said officials were combing the wreckage.
"We're trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter," said spokesperson Branden Silverman.

blocks.caption: The helicopter had been heading to the scene of this accident between a bus and an SUVImage: KABC-TV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cause of crash unknown
The local affiliate of US broadcaster NBC confirmed the helicopter was NewsChopper4, which had been en route to cover a deadly collision between an SUV and a city bus that killed two people.
There has been no immediate confirmation of the identity of those on board the helicopter, however, NBC reported it has been unable to contact the crew.
Reporters at the scene of the bus accident said the helicopter crashed about a mile (1.6 kilometers) away.

The fire department said dozens of firefighters had been dispatched to the incident and quickly extinguished the flaming wreckage. Aerial footage showed remains of the tail and rotor among storage containers and vehicles.

blocks.caption: Another news helicopter captured this image with pieces of the helicopter seen after firefighters doused the flamesImage: KABC-TV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have launched an investigation into what caused the crash.
Helicopters are frequently used in Los Angeles to provide live aerial coverage of news events in the second largest city in the US.

articles.title: [In the Public Square] The trial of Sara Duterte: So who’s watching now?
articles.summary: Does the public care? Is anyone watching?

blocks.text: Does the public care? Is anyone watching?

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte seems to follow a certain pattern. We might think of it as Netflix seasons: The first one ran for nine trial dates, involved Article IV, on grave threats, and ended before the State of the Nation Address. The second ran for 14 trial dates, involved Article I, on confidential funds, and ended abruptly with a call for amici curiae. This week, the third season started, involving unexplained wealth.
The question is: Does the public care? Is anyone watching?

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by the managing director of Fifty5Blue Jay Bautista, to make sense of the public’s interest on the impeachment trial.

articles.title: Redmi Note 17 Pro Series: How much battery do you really need?
articles.summary: I tried both the Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G and Redmi Note 17 Pro Max 5G, and after using them, the biggest difference I noticed came down to one thing: battery. Durability I could actually test The…

blocks.text: I tried both the Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G and Redmi Note 17 Pro Max 5G, and after using them, the biggest difference I noticed came down to one thing: battery.
Durability I could actually test

The weather has been unpredictable lately, and I got to put the phones’ durability to use. There were times when I got caught in sudden rain while booking a ride or checking directions, and normally I’d be hunched over trying to shield my phone with my body or putting it inside my bag so it wouldn’t get drenched.

With the Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G and Pro Max 5G, I was more comfortable keeping my phone out when I needed it. Both have IP66, IP68, IP69, and IP69K ratings, 3-meter drop resistance, and Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2.

The two phones are more or less the same when it comes to durability, so for me, that wasn’t really a reason to pick one over the other. I liked having that extra peace of mind, especially when I’m already trying to deal with the rain and everything else going on around me.
The biggest difference is the battery
This is where the two phones really separate themselves. The Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G has an 8,340mAh battery, while the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max 5G has a 10,000mAh battery.

The 8,340mAh battery on the Pro 5G is already a lot for my usual day. I’m constantly using my phone for work, messages, social media, watching videos, checking things online, and plenty of other little tasks.
But after using the Pro Max, I understood why having a 10,000mAh battery could be useful.

With my personal use, I was able to get almost three days of battery life. I was chatting with people, playing games, and spending quite a bit of time watching Chinese dramas on TikTok. I wasn’t specifically trying to conserve battery either. That was just how I normally used the phone. Because my phone is essential to me, I noticed the difference.

I usually think about my battery throughout the day. If I’m going somewhere for several hours, I’ll make sure my phone is charged before leaving. If I’m going to be away from an outlet, I’ll start thinking about whether I should bring a power bank.
With the Pro Max, I found myself checking the battery percentage much less often.
RELATED STORY: How to turn your smartphone into a gaming console
So, which one makes more sense?
After using both, I don’t think the biggest difference is durability. They’re quite similar in that area, and I was able to see that for myself while using them during unpredictable weather.
For me, it really comes down to how much battery you want.

The Pro 5G’s 8,340mAh battery is already more than enough for regular daily use. But if you’re someone like me who spends a lot of time on your phone and doesn’t want to think about charging as often, the Pro Max’s 10,000mAh battery is the feature that stands out.

I appreciated the Pro Max most for that reason. Nearly three days of my normal usage meant one less thing I had to think about, and when your phone is something you rely on throughout the day, that can make a surprisingly big difference.
The choice comes down to battery life

Overall, the REDMI Note 17 Pro 5G and Pro Max 5G offer a similar experience, with the biggest difference coming down to battery capacity. The Pro packs an 8,340mAh battery, while the Pro Max goes up to 10,000mAh.

articles.title: Cotabato City, Basilan name winners for parliamentary district seats
articles.summary: The winning candidates for the parliamentary district representative seats in Cotabato City and Basilan have been named following the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 1:28pm

The winning candidates for the parliamentary district representative seats in Cotabato City and Basilan have been named following the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
The BARMM Parliament has 80 seats, with 40 allocated to party representatives, 32 to district representatives and eight to sectoral representatives.

Of the 32 district seats, nine are for Lanao del Sur, five each for Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, four each for Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, three for Cotabato City, and two for the Special Geographic Area (SGA).
Cotabato City
The winning candidates in the three parliamentary districts of Cotabato City are:

items: Romeo Sema (MP) – first district
Naguib Sinarimbo (BFP) – second district
Tomanda Antok (BFP) – third district

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) secured two of the three district seats in Cotabato City, while Sema of the Mahardika Party (MP) won the first district.
Basilan
The winning candidates in Basilan are:

items: Rima Hassan (BFP) – first district
Pai Sali (UBJP) – second district
Abrar Hataman (BFP) – third district
Jay Hataman (BFP) – fourth district

blocks.text: The BFP secured three of the four district seats in Basilan, while the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) won one.
Voting in 36 of the 86 precincts in Maluso, Basilan was continued on Tuesday, September 15, after the Commission on Elections (Comelec) discovered pre-shaded ballots in the affected precincts.

Comelec spokesperson John Rex Laudiangco said on Tuesday that the individual behind the pre-shading of ballots in the 36 polling precincts would face electoral sabotage charges, which carry a penalty of life imprisonment.
Authorities were also identifying the candidates allegedly involved in the pre-shaded ballot incidents, as they could face disqualification, according to Comelec.
Comelec Chairperson George Erwin Garcia said the final voter turnout for the first BARMM parliamentary elections was 84.34%.

articles.title: Sydney man who allegedly called 13-year-old Muslim girl a ‘terrorist’ berates judge after bail refused
articles.summary:
Omar Yassine was arrested and charged with stalking and intimidation after allegedly hurling insults at year 8 student wearing a hijab

  • Get our

blocks.text: A middle-aged man accused of a “disgusting” Islamophobic attack on a 13-year-old girl has berated a judge after he was denied bail
Omar Yassine made an eventful court appearance on Wednesday after being held by police overnight for allegedly verbally abusing the Muslim schoolgirl on a Sydney bus.
Yassine told the court he had “hurled a few insults” at the girl, her friends and someone he thought was a teacher on Thursday but claimed he had not been the instigator.
“I didn’t threaten or intimidate anyone,” the 50-year-old, who did not want legal representation, said from the Bankstown local court dock on Wednesday.
“All I did was raise my phone ... a person alleged I took a photo [of them].
“There were four students hurling threats and abuse at me.”
The police prosecutor said there was strong evidence against Yassine, who the court heard had a 46-page criminal record.
The evidence included a video, recorded by the 13-year-old girl on an inner-western Sydney bus, that showed Yassine calling her a barrage of names, the prosecutor said.
The year 8 student, who was wearing a hijab and her school uniform, was allegedly called a “fucking terrorist” and an “immigrant dog” among other insults in the clip, later shared online.
The girl and other passengers reported the tirade to police after getting off the bus at Strathfield station.
Officers arrested Yassine at a home in nearby Greenacre after the girl and her mother went public about the incident on Tuesday.
He was charged with stalking and intimidation with intent to cause fear.
In the video, the teen told the man she was born in Australia and reminded him of her young age, but that didn’t stop the alleged abuse.
The girl and her mother told the ABC the incident was “really disgusting”.
In court, Yassine repeatedly interrupted the police prosecutor and acting judge Gary Still.
The 50-year-old said he should be released on bail because he would be able to report to police and was not a risk of committing another serious offence.
Judge Still disagreed.
after newsletter promotion
“This is a vulnerable victim, a 13-year-old on public transport,” the judge said.
“There are a number of matters on your record ... and you are just off a community corrections order.”
Upon being refused bail, Yassine turned his disdain on the judge.
“You’re pre-empting my behaviour ... how did you come up with that conclusion?” Yassine said as he was led off to the cells.
“Good work, Your Honour – bow down to them, mate.”
The abuse allegedly began after the 13-year-old stood up for another girl in a hijab who believed Yassine was taking photos of her without her knowledge.
The Strathfield state MP Jason Yat-sen Li said he was “horrified and deeply angry” about the alleged incident, while congratulating the teen for speaking up.
“Let me be absolutely clear: Strathfield will not tolerate racist or Islamophobic abuse, particularly when it targets children,” he said.
Yassine was not required to enter a plea and will return to court at a later date.

articles.title: PNP intensifies probe into BARMM violence, vows charges vs suspects
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine National Police (PNP) steps up its investigation into gun attacks, explosions, and other incidents and vows charges against suspects during the historic…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine National Police (PNP) steps up its investigation into gun attacks, explosions, and other incidents and vows charges against suspects during the historic Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections.
In a statement on Wednesday, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said authorities obtained leads that could help identify some of those involved and he expects charges to be filed soon.
“There are still a handful of individuals in the region who think the old ways still work, we proved them wrong,” said Nartatez.

“Now, they have to face the consequences of their actions as a strong message that such a violent mindset has no place in a democratic society which the people in BARMM upheld through the successful parliamentary elections,” he added.
Gun attacks and explosions were reported in Basilan, Cotabato City and Maguindanao del Sur during the elections, and an improvised explosive device was also recovered.
After some board of election inspectors considered withdrawing from their duties, police officers trained in election procedures were deployed.

Commission on Elections chair George Erwin Garcia previously said that the replacement police officers underwent proper training and received certification from the Department of Science and Technology to operate the Automated Counting Machines.
“We utilized about 2,000 SEBs (Special Electoral Boards) when our teachers withdrew,” Nartatez told reporters in an ambush interview.
“We deployed over 839 in Lanao del Sur and an additional 200-plus in the city of Cotabato, as well as in parts of Basilan particularly in Maluso,” he added.
Police units were instructed to continue securing BARMM throughout the election period, which runs until Sept. 29.
Despite security challenges, Nartatez earlier said that “BARMM elections were peaceful and orderly in almost all parts of the region.” /jpv

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthis target Mecca, warns of 'red line'
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses had destroyed a Houthi-deployed drone just outside the holy city of Mecca — a claim Houthis were quick to deny.

image.caption: The Saudi-Houthi conflict has opened up another front in the ongoing Middle East warImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: A Saudi Arabia-led military coalition battling Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Mecca on Wednesday, sparking outrage throughout the Muslim world amid the ongoing Middle East conflict.

"The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.
According to the statement, the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone "launched by the Terrorist Houthi Militia" before it entered the airspace of the holy city.
Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and in the kingdom's southern region which borders Yemen.
Houthis seize Red Sea chokepoint: What can Saudi Arabia do?
How did the Houthis respond?
The Houthis were quick to reject the coalition's claims as a "lie."
"The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone," Hazem al-Assad, a high-ranking member from the Houthi movement, wrote on X.
Meanwhile the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a bloc of 57 Muslim nations, condemned the "henious" attack.

The OIC General Secretariat "stresses that the violation of the sanctity of the holy sites is an unacceptable and intolerable transgression that requires deterring the perpetrators and blocking the path of anyone who dares to infringe upon these sites," it said in a statement.
Why are Saudi forces in conflict with the outhis?
Saudi Arabia is being increasingly affected by the rapidly escalating conflict across its southern border in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injured 13 people on Monday night, bringing the total number of people injured since the conflict escalated in July to about 100.

In July, the Houthis also blocked Saudi oil shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Houthi attacks in Yemen open dangerous new Middle East front

With the kingdom under attack, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday reached out to Egypt for support against Yemen's Houthi rebels. The leaders called for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
The growing escalation has opened up another front in the Middle East, which is already grappling with the US war on Iran.
Amid the latest development, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday issued an advisory asking its citizens to "reconsider travel" to the kingdom.
It warned of the "risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans and local laws regarding social media activity."

articles.title: Anthropic to build $31bn datacentre in western Queensland, David Crisafulli says
articles.summary:
Premier describes deal as ‘major win’ that will deliver more jobs for the state and put more energy into its grid

Anthropic, the AI giant behind the large language model Claude, has done a…

blocks.text: Anthropic, the AI giant behind the large language model Claude, has done a deal to lease the site of its first Australian datacentre in western Queensland.
The state premier, David Crisafulli, announced the decision in parliament on Wednesday.

The proposed Western Downs digital park is to be built by Singapore-based Zerra DC near Dalby, north-west of Toowoomba, and will connect to the Braemar power station. It is planned to open next year at a reported cost of $31.9bn.
Crisafulli told parliament that he had met with Anthropic during a trade mission and had outlined “why Queensland was the place to invest, with energy security and a streamlined approval process”.

“To have secured Anthropic’s first major investment in Australia is a massive show of confidence in Queensland,” he said. “It’s a major win that will deliver more jobs and put more energy into Queensland’s grid.”

The state, along with the Northern Territory, rejected a commonwealth push in July to make new AI centres use renewable energy. The state government claims to have won a carve-out from a national deal, allowing it to use the state’s coal generators to power them.
Crisafulli said Anthony Albanese had made a “commonsense decision” to “allow Queensland to chart its own path for power supply”.
“[Datacentre development] must add energy generation to the grid and drive down power prices for Queenslanders,” he said.

“It must protect local water supplies, and it must respect the communities where these centres go … we’ll do it in the right locations, and we’ll do it in the right way. Communities will have a say, just as they now do for projects like wind, solar, and batteries.”
after newsletter promotion

The Albanese government is weighing up a proposal to give AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default – a deal the independent senator David Pocock said would throw creatives “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.
Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, on Tuesday reiterated his call for a slowdown of AI development amid rising concern about artificial intelligence.

articles.title: Senate impeachment court is not under SC -- ex-SC Justice Puno
articles.summary: Retired Supreme Court (SC) Chief Justice Reynato Puno said Wednesday that the Senate impeachment court is not under the Supreme Court (SC) and that there is no provision under the 1987 Constitution…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 1:08pm

Retired Supreme Court (SC) Chief Justice Reynato Puno said Wednesday that the Senate impeachment court is not under the Supreme Court (SC) and that there is no provision under the 1987 Constitution explicitly allowing the SC to review the rules of the impeachment court.
Puno was one of the experts invited as an amici curiae or friend of the court to provide his expert opinion on the vote threshold needed to convict an impeached official.

“The impeachment court is not under the SC. The senator-judges are not like the judges of the regular courts of law who are all under the supervision of the SC,” he said during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
“It is for this reason, your honors, that the Senate impeachment court was granted judicial power,” he added.
He cited Article XI, Section VI of the Constitution, which states: “The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment.”
“Please note the use of the word sole, which means the only body that can try and decide all cases involving impeachment,” he said.
“The sole power to try and decide necessarily includes the lesser power to promulgate the rules that will govern the trial and decision of impeachment cases,” he added.
Puno stressed that the impeachment court’s judicial power was not granted under Article VIII of the Constitution, which covers the powers of the High Court.

“Nowhere does it explicitly appear in Article [VIII] that the SC can review the rules of the Senate impeachment court. Nowhere does it appear in Article [VIII] that the SC can review how the Senate should conduct its trial,” he said.

“Nowhere does it appear in Article [VIII] that the SC can review the evidence of the parties given in the impeachment court. Nowhere does it appear in Article [VIII] that the SC can review how the Senate impeachment court should decide impeachment cases,” he added.
According to the retired chief justice, it is up to the senator-judges toe decide whether they will change the number of judges needed for a conviction.
“In general, all these questions are to be resolved alone by the Senat e impeachment court because it is the sole judge to try and decide impeachment cases,” he said.
The 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."

According to Puno, there are two schools of thought in interpreting a constitutional provision. He said one follows the principle verba legis non est recedendum, which means “from the words of the law, there shall be no departure.”
However, he said another school of thought adopted the contextual or holistic approach.
Puno said this approach requires the interpretation of other related and relevant provisions of the constitution to determine the intent and purpose of the people. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Race for BARMM’s top post could turn into Marcos-Duterte proxy war
articles.summary: The scramble for 41 votes in the BARMM parliament tests whether the Macacua and Murad groups can reconcile or whether the struggle could eventually become a potential arena for a Marcos-Duterte…

blocks.text: The scramble for 41 votes in the BARMM parliament tests whether the Macacua and Murad groups can reconcile or whether the struggle could eventually become a potential arena for a Marcos-Duterte showdown

items: The race for the Bangsamoro region’s first chief minister hangs in the balance, with no single party able to govern alone.

The rivalry between the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) reflects deeper divisions within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), with former leaders now on opposing sides after a leadership change in 2025.

The outcome of the negotiations for control of the regional government could have significant implications for the 2028 presidential elections in the Philippines, as national political forces may become involved in the local power struggle.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The election is over, but the real fight for power in the Bangsamoro region may just be beginning.

The contest for the region’s first elected chief minister is likely to unfold over the next few weeks as rival political camps try to assemble the 41 votes needed to control the new parliament. And what began as a bitter split within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) could now become entangled with the much larger political struggle between President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte in the context of the 2028 presidential elections.

It could become, in effect, a proxy war played out in the Muslim-majority region between two national political forces, with the shape of the region’s first elected government at stake before the new parliament takes office next month.

blocks.caption: No single party gets majority of first-ever elected Bangsamoro Parliament

blocks.text: The September 14 elections produced a regional parliament in which neither of the two dominant parties can govern alone. The five-month-old Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), led by Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua, won 16 of the 40 regional party seats. The MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), led by MILF chairman and former BARMM interim chief minister Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, won 15.

The BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC), the party established by the region’s long-entrenched political families, ranked third. But the numbers have transformed the BGC and other smaller regional parties from supporting players into potential kingmakers.

Together, the BFP and UBJP have 61 (party and parliamentary districts) of the 80 seats; the remainder would be filled by the other parties and sectoral representatives. If the BFP and UBJP put aside their differences (which doesn’t seem likely at the moment) and form a coalition, then the “boxing bout is over” this early.

In that scenario, the MILF could emerge as the biggest beneficiary of an election that appeared to pit one faction against another. Both parties are led by former MILF figures who fought in the struggle that led to the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Macacua and Murad may now lead rival camps, but at their core, both are products of the MILF’s decades-old struggle.

Therefore, a reconciliation would mean that, beneath the rivalry and political realignment, the movement that fought for the Bangsamoro could retain decisive influence over its first elected government. If that happens, then the MILF, in the end, is the big winner.

Macacua and Murad are rivals because of a rupture within the MILF. In March 2025, Marcos replaced Murad as interim chief minister with Macacua, then the MILF’s armed group chief. The leadership change deepened tensions, and several formerly high-ranking MILF figures subsequently jumped from the UBJP to the BFP.

Macacua eventually left the UBJP, first becoming an independent candidate before taking over as BFP leader a month before the election. The MILF central committee later stripped him and several allies of their positions in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces.
Now, he and Murad will sit in the same elected parliament. They can carry on their feud. Or they can find a way to govern together.
But if they do not, the BGC’s and other group’s seats could become decisive.

There are already signs that BGC may be leaning toward Macacua. But that is not a settled outcome. Knowing how Philippine politics work, a move toward UBJP cannot be ruled out. If BGC joins Murad’s camp, the UBJP would have a potential route to the majority with support from other lawmakers.
BARMM has just entered the period of gapangan, the mad scramble for political support.
The election has supplied the numbers. Now comes the bargaining, and that could acquire a national dimension.

Macacua is closely associated with the Marcos administration — it was the President who turned Murad’s former senior minister and MILF armed wing top commander into BARMM interim chief minister. In 2022, Macacua is said to have supported the presidential bid of Marcos, while the MILF leadership openly backed then-vice president Leni Robredo.

Although he lost the top BARMM post to Macacua via presidential appointment, Murad has remained aschairman of the MILF and the leading figure of the UBJP. If the two camps clash over the chief minister’s post, the Marcos and Duterte forces could see the coalition negotiations as another arena in which influence can be gained or lost. Whoever controls the regional government would be in a strategic position to influence the outcome of the 2028 presidential elections in the BARMM.
The Duterte camp, in particular, could have an incentive to work against Macacua in the election because of his ties to Marcos.

That does not mean that every politician who opposes the BFP is a Duterte ally. Bangsamoro politics has its own alliances, political families, and local calculations that do not always follow the divisions in Manila — or Davao.
But if BFP and UBJP remain locked in their fight, the national divide could become harder to keep outside the room of the BARMM.

A BFP-UBJP reconciliation could keep the center of gravity within the Bangsamoro, bringing two rival MILF factions into one governing arrangement. But a prolonged fight could do the opposite, pulling BGC and the other smaller blocs deeper into the contest and giving national political forces more reason to take an interest.

In the next few weeks, the question will be who can get at least 41 votes, who is willing to make the necessary bargains and whether the struggle remains a Bangsamoro dispute or becomes an arena for a Marcos-Duterte showdown.

The first elected BARMM government of the Bangsamoro will take office next month. Before then, its government may be decided in the backroom negotiations now beginning. Or, it may have already been decided. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Anywhere, anytime’: Victoria police and PSOs to get random stop and search powers after Labor backflip
articles.summary: Premier Ben Carroll adopts Coalition’s stance on Jack’s Law, which gives police and PSOs power to randomly search people for knives with metal detectors The Victorian premier has made another policy…

blocks.text: The Victorian premier has made another policy backflip, announcing a re-elected Labor government would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors – despite experts warning of a lack of evidence that the measure reduces violent crime.

Ben Carroll on Wednesday announced he would match a commitment made by the Coalition opposition last year to introduce Queensland’s Jack’s Law, named after 17-year-old Jack Beasley, who was fatally stabbed in Surfers Paradise in 2019.

Under Labor’s commitment, police and PSOs would receive 1,200 extra handheld metal-detecting wands to use on any person in a public place from early next year. Or as the police minister, Paul Edbrooke, put it: “Anywhere, anytime.”
The bipartisan support for the new powers comes despite warnings from criminologists and human rights advocates that the laws will be ineffective at reducing violence.

Sarah Schwartz, the legal director of the Human Rights Law Centre accused Carroll of “ignoring the evidence and caving into pressure in a race to the bottom to suppress democratic freedoms and human rights”.

“We know from other states that these powers only serve to give police unchecked powers to harass and target people, particularly marginalised groups, while doing nothing to actually keep communities safe,” she said.

A Griffith University study of a 12-month trial of Jack’s Law on the Gold Coast between 2021–22 found there was no reduction in violence as a result of the searches and that they put human rights at risk.

“There’s no evidence that it’s in any way effective in actually reducing knife related violence, which is the whole premise of the law,” Griffith University’s Janet Ransley told the Guardian last year.
Swinburne University criminologist Joel McGregor said “tough-on -crime policies” would do little to address the causes of crime, particularly among young people.

“Police might find a knife or a weapon and they remove that weapon from the street. That’s a great outcome, but it doesn’t address the underlying behaviours as to why that person is carrying the knife or the weapon in the first place,” he said.

Currently in Victoria, police are only authorised to perform warranties pat-down searches in “designated areas.” A six-month designation of the CBD as one was earlier this year deemed invalid by the federal court.
Carroll said the government would work with legal experts to ensure Jack’s Law would be “watertight”.
“Victorians are sick of knife crime, and so am I,” he told reporters.

Jack’s Law has also been replicated in Tasmania, Western Australia and the Northern Territory following advocacy by Jack’s parents. In New South Wales, the warrantless search powers apply only in declared designated areas.
Victorian Labor’s move marks a significant shift for the state government after it had resisted expanding search powers under former leader Jacinta Allan.
After meeting with Beasley’s parents in September 2025, the then-police minister Anthony Carbines said the state’s search powers were sufficient.
after newsletter promotion
“It might not be called Jack’s Law, but what we have in place in Victoria is a safe and effective mechanism that Victoria police asked for,” he said at the time.
Asked repeatedly why there had been a policy change, Carroll answered “I’m the new premier”.
The Victorian Greens’ justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey said the about face showed Labor had “completely lost its way on community safety” and was “just copying whatever the Liberals announce.”

According to Queensland police statistics, police stopped and scanned 160,997 people between 18 July 2025 and 30 June 2026. More than 77% of them were male, and 22.6% of people with a known ethnic origin were Indigenous, despite Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people making up only 4.6% of Queensland’s population.
In Victoria, two years of data obtained by Liberty Victoria revealed just over 1% of the searches conducted in designated areas found illicit items, including weapons.
But Carroll’s shift was welcomed by Jack’s father, Brett Beasley, who said it was “about bloody time”.
“I’ve been pushing for Jack’s Law to be introduced down there for some time now, so it’s great news,” he told ABC Radio Melbourne.
“Put the politics aside and let’s focus on the community safety and that’s what Jack’s Law is all about.”
Additional reporting by Andrew Messenger

articles.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
articles.summary: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in…

blocks.text: The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.

Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.

The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.

blocks.caption: Wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank of England’s initial capital, according to Dr Michael Bennett.  Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.

“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.
“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”

An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge, the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.

The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind the Legacies of British Slavery (LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.

blocks.caption: The Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery.  Photograph: pawopa3336/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: The Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.
Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England had owned 599 enslaved people on two plantations.

An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.
The Bank also acknowledged and apologised for past governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.
Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29, was also an MP and defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.

Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an article published on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”

While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.
Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is building from Caribbean and African countries.
A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: Fresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debate
articles.summary: Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian…
articles.byline: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent. Photography by Wayne Crichlow

blocks.text: Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian case for reparative justice, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, visited the Ghanaian shore where he was enslaved as a boy.

After witnessing the dungeons beneath the chapel at Cape Coast Castle, once run by the Royal African Company (RAC), Mullally recommitted the Church of England to its “journey of repentance” for its role in slavery.

Back in Britain, historians working on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders were uncovering evidence that C of E clergy financed the RAC, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

The register, which documents investors in Britain’s nearly 250-year transatlantic slave trade, includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments helped fund hundreds of slaving voyages and a 1720 relaunch of the RAC. Among them was Henry Brydges, later a canon at St Paul’s Cathedral, who bought half of his £10,000 shareholding on the day he became the Archdeacon of Rochester.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register showed a “truly national picture”. Profits from enslavement filtered down to communities “from Cumbria to the Cotswolds” through bequests to parishes – evidence of a history of the C of E “giving slavery its blessing” and raising fresh questions about whether the church is doing enough to atone.

In 2023, church commissioners – the C of E’s asset managers – launched Project Spire, a £100m impact investment fund for communities affected by slavery’s legacies, which has caused division within the church. It is not a reparations fund, but is central to the church’s determination to be a force for justice and healing in the world. It was launched nearly 20 years after Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, rejected the idea that today’s church bears no responsibility for the past.

blocks.caption: The register includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments co-funded hundreds of slaving voyages. Among them was Henry Brydges, later canon of St Paul’s Cathedral, pictured.

blocks.text: However, Spire mainly responds to historic investments in the South Sea Company, which trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved Africans. That represents a “sliver of church complicity”, said Prof Alan Lester, a historical geographer at the University of Sussex.

That complicity helped shape modern Britain, Lester said. Plantation profits helped fuel the Industrial Revolution, railways, public health, welfare, universities, schools, church building and the public finances. “Look at Anglican parishes in Jamaica, their ability to withstand climate change, and compare that with the wealth generated in Britain by the plantation complex,” he said.
For the Rev Natasha Beckles, the dean of racial justice for Willesden, reckoning with this past goes to the heart of Christian faith.
“What was the purpose of the cross if we’re not able to talk about this?” she said. “Slavery made the image of God transactional. There has to be an understanding of the impact on the world.”

blocks.caption: ‘The public and people within the church don’t even know what the extent of the church’s involvement was,’ Dr Leona Vaughn says.

blocks.text: Dr Leona Vaughn of the University of Liverpool, a co-organiser of a 2025 Anglican “truth-telling” event, said: “The public and people within the church don’t even know the extent of the church’s involvement.

“We’ve not even started to come to terms with the ‘Slave Bible’,” she said, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible, stripped of liberation narratives, that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807.

The history of the United Society Partners in the Gospel (USPG), the C of E’s 325-year-old missionary partner, shows how powerful Anglicans practised and perpetuated transatlantic chattel slavery – a uniquely racialised, violent system of human commodification and forced mass migration. Today, members of USPG – of which Mullally is president – have committed to “the gospel’s call to break every chain of injustice”.

USPG’s forerunner, the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG), supplied chaplains to the RAC at Cape Coast Castle. For more than 120 years, with the involvement of C of E leaders, SPG enslaved people on the Codrington estate in Barbados, which generated the equivalent of £5m a year in today’s money.

At Codrington, enslaved Africans were branded with the word “Society”, tortured with the lash, straitjacket and iron collar, and worked to death. In seven months in 1746, 19 enslaved people died – including Daniel, who was “shot by accident” – with three deaths in a single day.
Pettigrew said the “clear signal” sent by the C of E’s relationship with Codrington was “if the church is doing it, why shouldn’t I?”
After abolition, SPG and at least 96 clergy who enslaved people received millions in compensation for “loss of property”. In 2023, USPG launched its own £7m reparative justice programme.

Christian collusion can be traced back to a 1452 papal bull authorising the enslavement of non-Christians, the author Malik Al Nasir said. He wants the C of E to digitise its records in the UK and the Caribbean.
after newsletter promotion

In the 17th century, John Cotton, a former Lincolnshire vicar, co-drafted a charter legalising slavery in New England. By the 1750s, high churchmen were codifying pro-slavery ideology: Thomas Newton, later the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, argued Africans were destined to be “servants of servants”, while Thomas Francklin, later the chaplain to George III, said: “We use [African] bodies for our support and happiness.”

blocks.caption: The London skyline from St Paul’s Cathedral, with the City in the distance. Experts say the C of E’s complicity in enslavement helped shape modern Britain.

blocks.text: Some Anglican voices did oppose slavery. Condemning it in 1685, the preacher Morgan Godwyn said: “We have … conspired with Satan.”

Project Spire’s critics have instead focused on the legacy of Anglican abolitionist MPs, such as William Wilberforce. Wilberforce’s 1823 anti-slavery petition was followed by his colleague Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton acknowledging that “we owe a large and liberal atonement”.

In his 1787 book, Cugoano – who won his freedom in England – wrote that the injustice done to Africans “cries aloud for universal reformation and national repentance”. He drew on biblical scriptures such as Numbers, Leviticus, Exodus and Deuteronomy that included reparative principles.

Class shaped church complicity, Beckles said. “The oldest child got the land, the second child they put in the church, the third was sent to the Caribbean.” That meant, Al Nasir said, that “one sibling could profit from slavery while another absolved it – the right hand washing the left”.
Enslaved African Christian leaders helped force the issue of abolition – including Samuel Sharpe, the deacon executed for leading Jamaica’s 1831-32 Baptist war.

The posthumously published Demerara diaries of the English Methodist the Rev John Smith also educated the British public about the relentless beatings, toil and meagre diet – raw yellow plantains – endured by enslaved Africans. Smith’s preaching was blamed by Anglican planters for Guyana’s 1823 Demerara rebellion. He died awaiting execution.

blocks.caption: Thomas Newton, who became the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, said in the 18th century that Africans were destined to be ‘servants of servants’.

blocks.text: The moral conviction of English non-conformists – such as Smith and Quaker abolitionists – contrasts with the 45 C of E clergymen in the register.

The C of E already has an impact investment fund, so insiders have expressed surprise at the backlash against Spire, which is facing a legal challenge. In the House of Commons in September, the MP Marsha de Cordova, the second church estates commissioner, rebutted claims from rightwing critics that Spire diverts money from English churches.

She said the church regarded historic links to slavery with profound regret, that Spire is funded from the commissioners’ own income rather than parish collections, and that the English ministry would receive £1.6bn over three years.

A 2023 report estimated Britain’s slavery debt at £18.6tn. For Beckles, no sum could be enough. “What do you say to a mother who has had her child taken from her? To talk about a figure is grotesque,” she said. “For that level of human suffering, you’d be writing a blank cheque.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: Revealed: the UK towns with the fewest jobs for young people
articles.summary: Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable…

blocks.text: Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work.

As ministers push to combat rising youth unemployment, the analysis from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) showed young people faced a tougher challenge in some parts of the country to find work than in others.

Publishing a new “local youth opportunity index” to track job vacancies across Britain, it said there was a sixfold gap in jobs in the South Yorkshire town compared with the more affluent Cotswolds, where there are fewer young adults but more opportunities.
Whereas Rotherham has 46 online job vacancies for every 1,000 young people, there are 288 in the area covered by Cotswold district council.
Highlighting deep regional divisions, the report found nine of the 10 best areas for youth job opportunities are in the south of England.

Places with job openings relative to the local youth population below the national average of 109, include East Renfrewshire in Scotland, Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, and Broxtowe in Nottinghamshire. Cities including Sheffield, Coventry and Cardiff also ranked near the bottom of the list for youth employment opportunities.
Places with the most opportunities included Woking in Surrey, Gloucester, Cherwell in Oxfordshire, and Warrington in the north-west of England.

The analysis comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness. The former Labour health secretary, who is expected to publish his findings next month before the autumn budget, has called for a policy overhaul involving education, welfare, and employment support.

Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet) surpassing 1 million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade.
Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill health and a tough jobs market.
after newsletter promotion

The IPPR said its report showed that becoming Neet was not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work. It urged ministers to prioritise overhauling the apprenticeship system and to create a new “work start” programme that would fund youth jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities. It also called for a new “youth allowance” that would replace different rates of universal credit benefits based on work capability.

Responding to the IPPR report, David Blunkett, the former Labour education secretary, said he had first-hand experience of the challenges facing young people from growing up on a Sheffield council estate and leaving school at 16 with no qualifications.

“Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future,” he said.

“We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open, and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.”

articles.title: People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder
articles.summary: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last…

blocks.text: Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.

Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.

Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.

blocks.caption: Asháninka territory in Brazil sits along the winding Amônia River. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

blocks.text: Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.

On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.

Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.

Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.

The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.

Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”

At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.

Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.

In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.

blocks.caption: An Indigenous person looks out over Apurímac River valley in Peru. Local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists have been threatened after calling for a more effective state presence across affected countries. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.

Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.

Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.

Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”
