articles.title: The Palestinian school under siege – podcast
articles.summary: At least five pupils at a village school in the West Bank have been killed in the last year by settlers and soldiers. Emma Graham-Harrison reports on how the school found itself…
articles.byline: Presented by Annie Kelly with Emma Graham-Harrison; produced by Ivor Manley and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli

blocks.text: Waheed Abu Naim is an English teacher at the Al Mughayyir boys’ school in a village in the West Bank. He loves his job, he says. “I am happy to be a teacher. Although we don’t get lots of money, because my students, especially in the morning, wait for me when I enter the school to shake hands, to smile at me while going inside their classes. So it’s a happy life.”

But the last year has been anything but happy for Waheed. His village is now surrounded by settlers, while the military has blocked off every road except one, which has a checkpoint on it. Teachers who live in neighbouring villages cannot always come to work. But worse are the attacks on the village by settlers.
In April, a 14-year-old pupil was killed next to a playground gate after a gunman opened fire. As Waheed rushed the teenager to hospital he learned his own brother had also been killed.

Senior Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison tells Annie Kelly: “We’ve documented the hundreds of children who’ve been killed by Israeli soldiers, settlers over the last three years. But even in that context, of sort-of regular deadly violence, there is something particularly horrific about someone taking aim at a school full of children.”

Four other students were also killed and, says Emma, things don’t seem to be getting better. “In the next few months I’m just, very unfortunately, expecting to see at least the same level of violence and frankly, probably an escalation.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia warns of ‘red line’ after Houthi drone intercepted close to holy city of Mecca
articles.summary:
The Iran-aligned militant group rejected the suggestion it had targeted Mecca, while the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the attack

Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, according to a ⁠spokesperson for the ⁠Saudi-led ​military coalition which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen.

The security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”, ⁠coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the ⁠Houthis.

Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest ​city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims ‌undertake each year.
Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, after what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017.

A Houthi official rejected the claim on Wednesday, with spokesperson Hazem al-Assad writing on X: “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned what they called a “heinous” attack on Islam’s holy city, blaming the Houthis. The group – which is made up of 57 Muslim-majority countries decried the “ongoing aggression against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.”

Saudi Arabia issued security alerts across parts of the country on Tuesday, including in Mecca and other ‌cities, following a week of attacks by Iran-aligned fighters that have drawn the kingdom deeper into the Middle East ​war.

The Houthis have seized control of parts of ⁠Yemen’s Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, one of the ​world’s most important ​shipping straits, threatening Saudi oil ​exports rerouted from the strait of Hormuz.
The group has ​announced several major ‌attacks on ​Saudi Arabia over ​the past week, including strikes on an airbase on Monday that it said were retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Human remains found in Arizona after deadly Grand Canyon flash floods
articles.summary:
Hiker Timothy Smith, 53, missing after late-August floods but officials decline to identify remains

Human remains have been discovered near Arizona’s Crystal Rapids, over two weeks after a…

blocks.text: Human remains have been discovered near Arizona’s Crystal Rapids, over two weeks after a flash flood tore through the Grand Canyon, leaving two people dead and one person missing.
National Park Service personnel recovered the remains, before transferring them to the Coconino county medical examiner’s office, the agency confirmed over email.

In late August, heavy rains brought a deluge of flood water barreling through the Grand Canyon national park. The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and a martial artist were recovered, according to the Associated Press. One hiker, Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old pilot from Wyoming, is unaccounted for.
The National Park Service did not identify who the remains belonged to, adding that no further information would be available at this time.
A Facebook account appearing to belong to the wife of the missing pilot, Carrie Smith, acknowledged the discovery of human remains.
“We ask that you continue to pray alongside us! Please be considerate of those handling the situation and those going through this difficult time,” Smith wrote in a Tuesday post.
In earlier Facebook posts, Smith described her husband as an outdoors aficionado.
“Tim loves to show us somewhere new and take us back to the places we love,” she wrote. “We know the search teams are working hard to bring Tim home to us.”

articles.title: Russia plotting to kill targets in US and Europe, federal officials say
articles.summary:
Intelligence services allegedly attempted to pay people to surveil and kill people perceived to be aligned with Ukraine

Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted…

blocks.text: Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the United States and in European nations supporting Ukraine, federal authorities said Tuesday as they announced charges against five people who remain at large.

An indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court said a network of the intelligence services had paid and attempted to pay individuals in the United States and in other countries to surveil targets to be killed with plans to then kill them.

The associates recruited in the network also had been solicited to carry out acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that were perceived to be aligned with Ukraine, the indictment said.

James Barnacle Jr, head of New York’s FBI office, said the FBI disrupted the plans “through relentless work” as members of the Russian intelligence services and their affiliates “conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world”.

Darren Cox, head of the Washington DC office of the FBI, cited “extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies that collectively disrupted Russia’s attempts to conduct violent acts in our nation’s capital and throughout the United States”.

He said in a release that when the threat was first identified, the FBI’s Washington field office and its partners “moved quickly to disrupt the plot and hold the Russian government accountable for its actions”.

According to the release, a network of people working for the Russian Federation’s intelligence services had since at least 2024 conspired to conduct and had conducted attacks and murders around the world, including within the United States.
It called the Russian intelligence services network “one arm” of the Russian Federation’s apparatus designed to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world.
Previously, the release said, the network had focused on Russian dissidents and defectors but most recently had targeted nations perceived to be allies of Ukraine.
Recently, it said, members of the network had tried to recruit multiple people in the United States.
Authorities said the network this summer recruited an individual based in the United States to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident it believed to be residing in the United States.

The indictment said a person identified only as “US Resident-1” had been sent to two locations associated with the targeted victim and was given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance” while being promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the work.

After conducting the surveillance and providing multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim to one of the men charged in the indictment, the US resident turned down the $40,000 that was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder.

When the offer was rejected, the member of the intelligence services who had made it tried to recruit multiple other people within the United States to do the job by offering them substantial amounts of money, the indictment said.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 8:47am
Former presidential spokesperson and congressman Harry Roque Jr. answers questions at the House of Representatives Quad Committee hearing on Aug. 23, 2024.
HREP

MANILA, Philippines (First published Sept. 15, 8 p.m.) — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Tuesday claimed that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque's asylum bid in Austria had been denied, a claim Roque later disputed.
Remulla made the statement during a press conference on Tuesday, September 15, adding that authorities would move against Roque once an Interpol Red Notice is issued.
"By the way, na-deny 'yung asylum ni Harry Roque," Remulla said. "Kapag may Red Notice na, kukunin ko siya."
By the way, Harry Roque's asylum bid was denied... I'll get him once there is a Red Notice.)
Remulla did not disclose further details about the purported denial. Philstar.com has also reached out to the Department of Justice for more information but has yet to receive a response.
Roque, who faces qualified human trafficking charges in connection with the raided Lucky South 99 POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, has been staying in Austria while seeking asylum.
An Angeles City court issued a warrant for his arrest in May 2025 over the non-bailable trafficking charges.
Roque left the Philippines without a recorded departure in Bureau of Immigration records after authorities began looking for him in 2024.
The Department of Justice had earlier issued an immigration lookout bulletin against him and several others in August 2024 in connection with the investigation into the Porac POGO hub.
Aside from the trafficking case, Roque also faces a tax evasion complaint filed by the Bureau of Internal Revenue before the DOJ.
In an interview with One News' "Storycon," Roque denied Remulla's claim, calling it "fake news."
Roque said his asylum application had already been submitted for resolution and that he was still awaiting a decision from Austrian authorities.
"The truth of the matter is it's been submitted and we continue to await for the decision of the asylum office," Roque said.

articles.title: Ex-Duterte vlogger RJ Nieto gets Palace assistant secretary post
articles.summary: Former pro-Duterte vlogger Rey Joseph “RJ” Nieto, who was behind the now-unpublished Thinking Pinoy blog, has been appointed assistant secretary at the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 8:46am
Blogger RJ Nieto, known as Thinking Pinoy, attends a Senate hearing on fake news on Oct. 4, 2017.
The Philippine STAR / Mong Pintolo

MANILA, Philippines — Former pro-Duterte vlogger Rey Joseph “RJ” Nieto, who was behind the now-unpublished Thinking Pinoy blog, has been appointed assistant secretary at the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.

In a letter dated Sept. 1, 2026, Marcos said Nieto may qualify and perform the duties of the office upon furnishing the Office of the President and the Civil Service Commission with copies of his oath of office.
Nieto confirmed his appointment in a Facebook post, where he shared his appointment letter and said he had yet to take his oath of office.
"There are still a few formalities to complete before I begin work," Nieto said.

He said Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos would decide his exact portfolio, adding that the Cabinet Secretary's office monitors whether government programs are being properly implemented and whether services are reaching the public.
Nieto said he is unlikely to work in communications, describing the position as not a spokesperson role.
"From what I understand, much of the work will be closer to my academic training. That suits me. Mahal ang Botox, kaya bawal ma-stress unnecessarily," he said.
Nieto became known for his Thinking Pinoy blog, which he started in 2015 and used to publish political commentary.
In October 2018, Nieto pleaded not guilty before the Pasay City Regional Trial Court Branch 111 to a libel complaint filed by then-Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV.
Trillanes accused Nieto of libel over a social media post claiming that then-US President Donald Trump had called Trillanes a “narco,” or drug lord.
Nieto was eventually acquitted in the case in June 2021.

In a separate case, blogger Jover Laurio, who ran Pinoy Ako Blog, filed a complaint against Nieto in 2018 over the publication of her personal information, including her full name, user credentials and law school.

The Makati Regional Trial Court Branch 132 later ruled in Laurio’s favor in the data privacy case. Nieto was ordered to pay P300,000 in damages and P50,000 in attorney’s fees and litigation expenses for violating the Data Privacy Act of 2012.
Nieto previously served as a part-time instructor at Bulacan State University and a columnist for Manila Bulletin.

He earned a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics with first-class honors from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom in June 2026. He is also pursuing a part-time MSc in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Public Policy at University College London.

"I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. Sana magamit ko iyon sa trabaho," Nieto said.
(I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. I hope I can use that in my work.)
He also acknowledged that he still has much to learn, saying, “government is not a classroom.”
"Marami pa rin akong kailangang matutunan," he said.
(I still have a lot to learn.)

articles.title: Supporting acts pull out of Ed Sheeran's tour over dropping Macklemore
articles.summary: Macklemore was dropped over his pro-Palestinian stance, amid accusations of antisemitism. Sheeran said removing the artist was not his decision but that of the tour's promoters.

image.caption: Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour has been shaken by a string of withdrawals over canceling Macklemore [FILE: Sept 9, 2024] Image: Carlos Elias Junior/Fotoarena/IMAGO

blocks.text: Singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran's North and South American leg of his Loop Tour was in trouble on Tuesday, as his supporting acts dropped out one after the other over the removal of rapper Macklemore from the lineup.
Macklemore said Monday that he was being dropped from the tour for his pro-Palestinian stance. Sheeran distanced himself from the decision on Tuesday, insisting the tour's promoters made the call.

blocks.caption: Macklemore said billionaire Robert Kraft was behind the movement that culminated with dropping him from Sheeran's tourImage: Jack Plunkett/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who dropped out of the Ed Sheeran tour and what did they say?
Irish acts Aaron Rowe and folk backing band Beoga announced they were leaving the tour, as did Danish band Lukas Graham and US artist Finneas, who is Billie Eilish's brother.

blocks.caption: Finneas was among those standing by Macklemore and thus withdrawing from Sheeran's tourImage: Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said on Instagram. "I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."
Rowe said he had not "made the decision lightly," stressing his friendship with Sheeran, whom he thanked for "chang[ing] my life."
"But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he wrote on Instagram.
Beoga also drew on their Irish background, saying on Instagram: "We are Irish people who understand colonialism."
"We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us," they wrote.
Lukas Graham also stressed it was a "difficult decision."

"Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," the band posted, in seeming reference to billionaire Robert Kraft's role in Macklemore's removal from the tour.
Why was Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran's tour?
Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after shouting "Free Palestine!" during the September 5 date at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium.

He was performing his protest song "Hind's Hall," about a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed during the Gaza war in 2024 after a recorded phone call with paramedics following her family's killing. The Israeli military last month ordered a criminal probe into her death.
"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you," Macklemore said during the concert.
Israeli officials have steadfastly rejected accusations of conducting a genocide in Gaza.

On Monday, Macklemore said several US venues where the tour was due to perform told the promoter they would prohibit him from opening for Sheeran, adding that Gillette Stadium owner Kraft had rallied the movement against him.

Kraft on Monday said the decision to cancel Macklemore's performance was a result of his recent comments "and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community."
Sheeran has, meanwhile, focused on distancing himself from the decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

The British singer insisted he would not take sides in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, "I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed."

articles.title: Scams, other cybercrimes rise to record 8% of families, says SWS
articles.summary: One in 12 Filipino families had a member fall victim to cybercrime in the past 6 months.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 8:31am
This undated photo illustration shows a mobile phone displaying a warning for a suspected scam or fraudulent call.
Illustration / Elena Uve

MANILA, Philippines — Eight percent of Filipino families had at least one member fall victim to cybercrime in the six months leading to June, the highest level recorded by Social Weather Stations since it began tracking the figure in 2023.
The June figure was up from 5.8% in March, even as the share of families affected by common crimes such as robbery, break-ins and physical violence declined nationwide.
Cybercrime cases among families rose sharply in Metro Manila, from 10.1% in March to 13.4% in June, and in the Visayas, from 4.1% to 10.4%, SWS said Monday, September 14.
The figure also increased in Mindanao from 5.3% to 8.8%.
Balance Luzon was the only major area to record a decline, from 5.5% to 5.1%.
SWS asked respondents whether they or any family member had fallen victim to online scams, account hacking, cyberbullying or other cybercrimes in the previous six months.
The survey was conducted from June 20 to 29 through face-to-face interviews with 1,200 adults nationwide, with 300 respondents each from Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
Common crimes decline
Meanwhile, 10% of Filipino families reported that at least one member had fallen victim to a common crime in the previous six months, down from 12.3% in March.
SWS classifies street robbery or pickpocketing, home break-ins, carnapping and physical violence as common crimes.
The Philippine National Police welcomed the decline while acknowledging the growing threat of crimes committed online.

"The PNP, through the Anti-Cybercrime Group... continues to strengthen its response to cyber-related offenses while reminding the public to remain vigilant against online scams, account hacking, cyberbullying, and other forms of digital victimization," the PNP said in a statement Monday.

articles.title: Anthropic’s CEO calls for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
articles.summary:
At San Francisco conference, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman calls for more rigorous security measures

Anthropic’s CEO took the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call…

blocks.text: Anthropic’s CEO took the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call for a slowdown of AI development, while Nvidia’s CEO argued against such deceleration.

Dario Amodei used an automotive analogy to make his point: when a competing car company has a safety incident like brake failures, it is a moment for all car companies to stop and review their own practices, he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention on Tuesday.

“It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.”
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after: “Run as fast as you can.”

Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies; coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries; and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and was “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps.

Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. Coxon’s comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public.

Huang, who also made an appearance at Dreamforce on Tuesday, said companies should not slow down AI development. He argued that new regulations were not necessary, advising AI companies to simply wait to release products until they know they are safe rather than begging the US government to intervene.

Huang said he envisioned a future where “every company, every enterprise … would become an AI company”. He said companies would become more ambitious when armed with AI and reiterated the idea that those who do not embrace the technology will get left behind.
He also pushed back on the idea that AI is going to destroy jobs, calling it “completely nonsense”.

One day prior at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, Donald Trump called Huang while the CEO was on stage. Huang put the president on speakerphone as Trump called the growing concern about AI a “hoax” and asserted again that a slowdown would only benefit China.
Huang responded: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America.”
Altman, who spoke later on Tuesday, called for a new level of rigor on security as AI advances.

Altman said AI models had advanced so quickly that monitoring and security need to be treated with a “new level of rigor”, calling an incident in which OpenAI agents hacked into another company a “wake-up call” for the industry. He also said the public was very “right to be afraid” of AI because of the potential loss of control, and the possibility of a small group of powerful AI companies exerting their views on the world.
People “feel the speed with which things are moving”, Altman said. “It doesn’t take as much imagination to imagine how this could go wrong.”
after newsletter promotion
Previously, Altman agreed with Amodei’s push for a slowdown. But at Dreamforce on Tuesday, he said he was disappointed with how the argument had been framed.

“You have companies saying things like: ‘We will only slow down or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible,’” he said, suggesting that this created fear for the public. “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing.”

Altman said the hacking incidents showed that companies needed to prepare for an “impending wave of cyber-attacks”, saying: “We are not that far away from open-source models that can do serious damage.” Companies should use this “little period of advantage to defend yourselves”, he said.

The rising concern over AI comes as OpenAI and Anthropic head for initial public offerings, which could give investors and the public insight into the companies’ finances. Some analysts have predicted the IPOs will be among some of the largest in history. Amid the AI panic, Altman said he planned to delay OpenAI’s IPO until next year over safety concerns.
On Tuesday, Amodei said what surprised him most about AI was the speed of its proliferation.

“It’s been the pace of the progress – not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he said about the growing adoption of AI. “We had a prediction of just how capable these models would be. But I think what we didn’t appreciate is that it would lead to these companies growing so fast.”

Regardless of the rapid pace of development, Altman said he believed people would use AI as a tool to benefit other people and grow their businesses. He said this moment represented a time when the “sci-fi” scenario came to fruition, where people were talking to their AI assistants and transforming the way they work.
“I think we’re going to stay in an extremely human-centric world, no matter how good the technology gets,” he said.

articles.title: Trump administration plans to resume deliveries of 2,000-lb bombs to Israel
articles.summary:
Delivery of the weapons had been halted two years ago over mass casualty concerns amid Israel’s bombing of Gaza

The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-lb bombs to…

blocks.text: The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000lb bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago.

The $2.8bn package includes 40,000 bombs, made up of 20,000 MK-84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to two US officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke on Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss the package, which is not yet final.

Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing – in which US taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.

The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israeli’s military capacity. The war on Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the territory. The US had brokered a fragile ceasefire, but it has been violated several times.

The package, which was reported earlier by the Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its war on Gaza in response to the deadly 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas.
In 2024, the Biden administration held off on one shipment of the bombs, but Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.

Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3bn sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67bn in January.
The 2,000lb bombs have multiple variants, with some designed to penetrate deep, underground targets while others detonate above ground and cause widespread damage.

Though the Israeli military has offered few details about what bombs and artillery it has used in Gaza, experts analyzing strike footage and blast fragments found on-site believe US-made bombs have been used there, targeting a tunnel network reportedly used by Hamas but also killing people in densely populated areas.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel in 2023 killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Israel has since killed more than 73,264 Palestinians, including those killed in violation of the ceasefire, Gaza’s health ministry said.

articles.title: #EmmysSoWhite again: No actors of colour win during 2026 Primetime Emmys
articles.summary: There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted…

image.caption: Host Mariska Hargitay speaks onstage during the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Monday. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted awards going to white performers.
All acting category winners during TV's biggest night were white
In 2015, activist and writer April Reign created the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag.
Now, she says she doesn't really watch award shows live, and last night's Emmys was an example of why.

There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Primetime Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted awards going to white performers.
"It's not a regression, it's definitely a stall," said Reign.

items: Emmys 2026 winners list: Widow's Bay, The Pitt take top honours

blocks.text: The other two major acting categories — supporting actor and supporting actress in a limited series — were given out last week at the Creative Arts Emmys, but those winners didn't change the tally.
'A pattern, not a moment'
By Tuesday morning, #EmmysSoWhite was trending, with users calling out the Television Academy on social media.

"The academy saw that three black women made history at the Emmys winning the big categories of the night and how happy everybody was and said never again," one user wrote on X, referencing the 2024 Emmy awards, "so now we’re stuck with #EmmysSOWhite for the foreseeable future 🫩"
"What is this... #EmmysSoWhite" wrote another, alongside a photo composite of the winners.

Reign started the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag in 2015, when all 20 acting nominees for the Academy Awards that year were white, sparking a conversation and a movement about the Academy and its voting body.
While there have been some changes in the following years aimed at addressing these discrepancies, Reign called out Monday's results.
"This is a pattern, not a moment," Reign said in an interview with CBC News. "A single snub is an accident. A pattern this consistent is a design feature of how the institution votes."

The Television Academy released a transparency report in February revealing that the majority of its members in 2026 — 67 per cent — were white. It publishes this report annually, with the first official one coming out in 2021.

At the same time, the academy pointed to steady year-over-year growth in its membership among people identifying as biracial, multiracial, East Asian and Southeast Asian, as well as women, non-binary, transgender and intersex voters.

items: 2026 Emmys: Widow's Bay upsets, The Pitt triumphs at Canada-preoccupied ceremony

blocks.text: Reign said the conversation around representation needs to begin long before awards season, pointing to the writers, casting directors and behind-the-scenes decision-makers who shape which stories and characters make it to the screen.

"We can't wait until we get to the award shows to have this conversation when, you know, the pipeline starts before a single word is written on the page," she said. She suggests asking questions like who the casting directors and show-runners are, and who is saying a white character couldn't be queer or a person of colour.

"Those are the questions that we need to ask from the very beginning so that we're not having these conversations again in February or March for the Oscars, and in September for the Emmys, because it's too late."

It's worth noting that outside of the primetime broadcast, Ernest Harden Jr. picked up an acting win Monday night for his guest-starring role as Louie Cloverfield on The Pitt. But the guest acting categories weren't presented during the broadcast. Octavia Spencer also won for narrating Lost Women of Alaska.

And while Monday night's show was a complete shutout for actors of colour, director Hiro Murai won a golden statuette for Widow's Bay. He's now the first Asian filmmaker to win best directing for a comedy series at the Emmys and only the third to win a primetime Emmy in any category, joining Emmy-winning directors Lee Sung Jin, who won for Beef, and Hwang Dong-hyuk, who won for Squid Game.
How does this compare to previous years?
Representation at the Emmys was actually down before Monday's ceremony even started.
Variety reports only 17 performers of colour scored acting nominations this year — a sharp drop from 28 last year.
The Emmys made headlines for diverse nominations in 2021, however every single lead and supporting acting winner that year ended up being white, also prompting the hashtag #EmmysSoWhite.
Let's look at how things have shaken out over the last few years for diverse winners at the Emmys.

Last year (2025): One of the 12 acting races went to a person of color — Tramell Tillman won for Severance and made history as the first Black man to take home outstanding supporting actor in a drama series.
2024: Four out of the dozen acting trophies went to diverse winners (including Liza Colón-Zayas, Lamorne Morris and Shōgun stars Hiroyuki Sanada and Anna Sawai).

2024 (January): This delayed ceremony was the peak of diversity for acting wins, with five actors of colour taking the stage to claim trophies: Quinta Brunson, Ayo Edebiri, Niecy Nash-Betts, Steven Yeun and Ali Wong.
2022: We saw three diverse performers win: Lee Jung-jae, Zendaya and Sheryl Lee Ralph.
2021: This was the last time all of the primetime acting winners were white.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte's camp concerned about Trillanes' links to ICC prosecution's 8 new incidents
articles.summary: Rodrigo Duterte"s camp concerned about Trillanes" links to ICC prosecution"s 8 new incidents
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 7:03am

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Lawyers of former President Rodrigo Duterte are asking the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to "determine the admissibilityof the eight new incidents included by the Office of the Prosecutor in its Trial Brief, while questioning their documentary evidence as "linked" to former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV.

Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes requests the Trial Chamber for a “judicial determination” of Incidents 50 to 57 mentioned by the prosecution in its 143-page Trial Brief—whether for the latter to file an amended version or remove the incidents entirely from the document.
Haynes argues that the eight new incidents were added by the prosecution without prior judicial authorization.

“In its Trial Brief, the Prosecution justified its addition of these eight new incidents as falling within the scope of the confirmed charges ‘because they were perpetrated in a ‘time during which and an area where criminal acts were allegedly committed by an identifiable group of perpetrators against an identifiable group of victims,’” Haynes said.
Evidence source

The Document Containing the Charges (DCC) specified 49 incidents in Duterte’s three counts of crimes against humanity. The prosecution’s Trial Brief now lists 57, with the additions at the center of the defense challenge.
Duterte’s defense team said it was notified by the prosecution of the new incidents through an email on August 31 regarding the latter’s submission of its Trial Brief.
Available information about the new incidents show that several happened in the National Capital Region and Region IV-A in 2016, or were victims on an “illegal drug personalities’ watchlist.”
The defense expressed concern over the authenticity and sources of evidence, which they linked to Trillanes, who is known as a critic of the former president.

“The chain of custody reveals that the documentary evidence cited in the Trial Brief in relation to the eight new incidents has a single political opponent of Mr Duterte, Antonio Trillanes, as its source, and these documents – which include purported internal PNP documentation – bear no indication of authenticity.”

In their argument, the defense claimed that Trillanes “has produced all of the newly disclosed PNP Incident Record Forms underpinning these eight incidents” despite having “no known legitimate means of accessing internal PNP documentation.”
Duterte’s lawyers also questioned the new Incident Record Forms for lacking signatures or “an official stamp indicating that they are a ‘certified true copy’ of the original.”

“In light of these evidentiary deficiencies, questions may be raised as to whether these eight incidents would have passed the lower standard of proof applicable at confirmation, had they been included in the original pre-confirmation brief and document containing the charges,” the defense argued.
Judicial oversight

Citing previous ICC cases that discussed adding incidents or amending charges before trial, Duterte’s defense argued that a trial chamber could authorize the prosecution to “add a victim without recourse to Article 61(9)” but not extend it to include a “new incident setting out a new time, place, individual criminal act, principal perpetrator, and victim.”
Haynes also added that “other criminal acts not mentioned in the document containing the charges” should “fall squarely within the facts and circumstances of the charges.”
“It is abundantly clear that judicial oversight is essential, and that the Prosecution cannot merely add to the confirmed charges proprio motu and without judicial authorisation,” Haynes said.
Timing of addition

The defense also submitted that the document containing the charges “no longer match” the current Trial Brief due to the eight new incidents, which they also argue “exceed the scope of the confirmation decision.”
”The Prosecution is now seeking to add eight new incidents based upon fresh evidence that constitute new material facts, not ‘further specification’ of the confirmed charges,” the defense argued.
They also questioned the timing of the prosecution’s addition of the new incidents, which were disclosed only around three months before Duterte’s trial is scheduled to start on November 30.
“Each incident rests upon fresh evidence and seeks to introduce an entirely new set of material facts, meaning authorisation is required,” Haynes said.
No public response from the Office of the Prosecutor to the defense submission has been published as of writing.
Trial Chamber III is also set to hold a status conference today. It remains to be seen whether the dispute over the eight additional incidents will be taken up during the hearing. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers
articles.summary:
More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says

About 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they…

blocks.text: About 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they try to balance their vulnerable relatives’ growing care needs with declining access to state-funded social care services.

Research estimates that more than a million people have left the workplace to look after ageing, ill and disabled loved ones in the past two years, highlighting the social challenges caused by UK’s rapidly changing demographic profile.

Unpaid caring is now a “widespread social and economic reality” for UK households, it says, with one in five employees – equivalent to 6.7 million people – facing career and financial sacrifices as they juggle paid work and care for family or friends.

Over a fifth of those surveyed (22%) had reduced their job hours to juggle work and care, with over a third (34%) working less than eight hours a week. Around one in 10 carers said they had turned down promotions or taken on lower-paid roles to stay in work.

Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy at Carers UK, said: “These figures represent real people who have had to make difficult decisions about their careers, their financial security and their futures due to the pressures of balancing work and care.”

Carers UK, which published the report, called on government to strengthen employment rights for unpaid carers, including introducing a statutory entitlement to 10 days’ annual paid carer’s leave for employees.

It urged Louise Casey’s independent review of adult social care, expected to report in the next few months, to recommend policy changes putting carers at the centre of a reformed system, by making it easier for carers to combine work and unpaid care.
Midwife Jacqui Hylton, aged 58, gave up her 30-year NHS career to become a full-time carer two years ago when her then 86-year-old mother Winnie’s health took a serious turn for the worse.

Hylton moved from Hertfordshire to Leeds to live with Winnie and become her full-time carer. But she is frustrated that her professional skills are going to waste when the NHS faces a midwife shortage.

Caring will make it harder for her to return to midwifery as she is unable to work the required number of hours a year to maintain her professional accreditation. Enhanced respite allowance would potentially enable her to keep her hand in at work.

“I don’t regret caring for my mum. But financially I’m worse off, my pension will be less than it should have been. It’s lonely at times and its extremely hard work – harder than working in the NHS,” she said.

The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Around one in five (20%) of UK adults, equivalent to 11 million people, report unpaid care duties.

As well as affecting carers’ finances, careers and wellbeing, the report estimates the doubling in the number of people quitting paid work to care over the past seven years comes at an annual £37bn economic cost to the UK.

A government spokesperson said: “Unpaid carers make an extraordinary contribution to families, our communities and the economy, and I would like to personally thank Carers UK for their invaluable work in supporting unpaid carers and championing the issues they face every day.

“We want to ensure there are good jobs for carers who want to work alongside managing their caring responsibilities. This is why we are exploring how best to support unpaid carers through our review of employment rights.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 26: What to expect
articles.summary: Legal luminaries will take center stage on Wednesday not as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, but as amici curiae, or friends of the court, who will help resolve…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 6:43am

Legal luminaries will take center stage on Wednesday not as witnesses in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, but as amici curiae, or friends of the court, who will help resolve questions on the conviction vote threshold.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said there will be no trial on Wednesday to give ample time to the four retired Supreme Court justices who will provide expert legal advice following the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict the Vice President.

Set to appear before the court to give their position on the matter and take questions from the senator-judges are three former magistrates — Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban, Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Reynato Puno, and Retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna.
Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. will also participate, but through a legal memorandum instead of a physical appearance.
Copies of Davide’s legal memorandum, as well as the position paper from San Beda University School of Law dean Fr. Ranhilio Aquino, were earlier given to senator-judges and the parties.
Escudero said that senator-judges will be given five minutes each to ask questions to all or either of the three amici curiae present.
The defense and prosecution counsels are likewise allowed to ask questions coursed through the presiding officer.

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said the amici curiae are expected to answer questions on whether the phrase “all the Members of the Senate,” as stated in Article XI, Section 3, Paragraph 6 of the Constitution, should refer to the Senate’s full membership of 24 senators or only those “who are legally and physically capacitated to participate and vote on the final question in an impeachment trial.”

The amici curiae are also set to face questions related to the Avelino v. Cuenco case, particularly whether its treatment of members beyond the Senate’s coercive jurisdiction applies to senators who are detained, abroad, suspended or whose whereabouts are unknown.
The questions will seek to determine whether such senators should be included in the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” for purposes of the two-thirds vote required under the Constitution.

They are also expected to give their views on whether a senator-judge who did not attend or substantially participate in the impeachment proceedings, including in propounding questions to and observing the demeanor of witnesses, may nevertheless validly cast a vote on the final question in an impeachment trial. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: AI leaders call for regulations, Trump dismisses 'hoaxes'
articles.summary: AI giants are working to create a standards body amid rising alarms about the dangers of the industry. Meanwhile, Trump has dismissed the warnings, and a divided US Congress has failed to act.

image.caption: Anthropic, Google and OpenAI say they are working on a self-regulatory body to supervise the fast-growing industry Image: IMAGO/ZUMA Press

blocks.text: Some of the top names in AI are working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers and an apparent US reluctance to police its speedy development.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI on Tuesday said it was working with top competitors Anthropic and Google on a self-regulatory body.

This comes amid rising calls for stricter control on the technology that is growing at lightning speed and not without dangerous precedents, calls that have thus far gone unanswered by the Donald Trump administration.
What do we know about the proposed self-regulatory body?
The regulatory body, proposed by Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, would be modeled after the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which oversees US brokers and investment firms.
Hassabis had called in July for a federal organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public.
He suggested funding would come from the industry to "attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing."
AI chatbot falsely accuses journalist of crimes
The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escalated in recent weeks amid warnings from two former workers at major AI developers.
Researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic last week, sounding the alarm that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."
On Monday, former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.
How has the US government under Trump reacted to the calls?
Trump has dismissed the calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy," while a divided Congress, narrowly controlled by Trump's Republicans, has failed to act.
The looming midterm elections make it unlikely any action will come soon despite AI and the power-hungry data centers needed to run it being a concern for many voters.

Trump's dismissal has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.
The dire prediction that AI could destroy humanity "is not grounded on science," Huang said.
Leading Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have, however, expressed caution.
Amid Washington's persistent apathy toward regulation, smaller AI companies have warned any self-regulatory measures would come at their expense.
Canadian AI company Cohere's chief, Aidan Gomez, has accused the dominant American AI labs of forming a "cartel" under the guise of safety.

"AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting," Gomez wrote in a blog post on Sunday.
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?

articles.title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds
articles.summary:
Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild

The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of…
articles.byline: Joseph Gedeon and Andrew Roth in Washington

blocks.text: The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls.

The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”.

The Pentagon’s report did not address an internal Pentagon investigation into the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people, including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying the results of the investigation that would show negligence by the Pentagon in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes.

The new $38bn estimate in the CBO report, which is some of the first public accounting of the cost of the war in Iran, was requested by the Democratic congressman Brendan Boyle, ranking member of the House budget committee. It also found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. And it estimated that the cost would grow $3bn for every additional month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation.

Much of that cost has come from missile defenses. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and Navy interceptors that CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”.

In a White House statement responding to reports of the shortage, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, separately dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true” in August.

According to the CBO report, the shortage would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains such an arsenal and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has.

Munitions have been the single largest driver of the Pentagon’s costs overall, CBO found: $21.7bn to replace weapons expended so far, of which $13.1bn went toward missile defense interceptors alone. The office also put a price on damage to American aircraft and equipment, including a destroyed Thaad radar system, and said it was forced to build its estimates largely from public reporting because the Pentagon did not respond to its requests for information.

The report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been.
It also said that the war had led to the “large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years”.

In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out (including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs), $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs CBO could not examine – a far larger share of secret funding than in past war supplementals.
CBO further added that it still cannot estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

articles.title: Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to steal a UCP riding in Calgary
articles.summary: It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.

image.caption: Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi talks about his candidate's byelection victory on Tuesday, as MLA-elect Kyle Campbell looks on. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.
A surprise upset 5 weeks before referendum, and a whole year before next election
In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.
No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.
The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.
The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.

“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.
It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.
We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.
Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.

Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.

Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.

The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”

After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.

Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.

How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.
After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”
“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.
Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.
In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.

In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.
Ample time to interpret message

That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.

Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.

Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.

It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.

The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel, with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.

The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

The outspoken senator criticised Donald Trump’s potential forever war with Iran while singling out Hanson’s support of his actions.
double quotation markYou’d put [Australian soldiers] back in another American forever war? [Hanson] is not only dangerous, she’s delusional!
Lambie said figures such as Trump and Nigel Farage were great at telling people they would fight for them while doing the opposite.

double quotation markSenator Hanson will be fine in her retirement, as will Nigel and Donald in theirs, because once again they are feathering their own nests ... Australia can choose not to follow the ugly politics of populism, we can do better because we bloody are better. And it’s not about right or left, it’s about respect and finding solutions, and not operating from a place of fear – whatever side you’re on.

blocks.text: Gambling company fined $1m for sending 800 messages to 165 people on Betstop

blocks.caption: Henry Belot

blocks.text: Henry Belot

Betting company Dabble has been fined more than $1m for continuing to send more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority also found the gambling company failed to close the betting accounts of 157 people who registered with Betstop, which helps people break their gambling addictions.
In a statement, ACMA said Dabble sent more than 2000 push notifications to 45 customers without including any information about the Betstop service, which is a legal requirement.
The watchdog has fined the company $1,069,200. According to Acma, Dabble has also given a court-enforceable undertaking to guarantee future compliance with the rules.
Acma member, Carolyn Lidgerwood, said the breachers were serious and undermined the federal government’s harm minimisation strategy.

double quotation markPeople who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering. Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions. BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules. The Acma will take action where wagering providers fail to meet their obligations.
Renters in NSW will be able to transfer their bond from one property to the next from today, meaning they won’t need to come up with thousands of dollars upfront every time they move.
It’s expected Smart Rental Bonds will save more than two million renters across the state up to $4,000 each time they move home – though the online scheme costs $25 to use.
The NSW government will pay the landlord the bond upon the end of the lease, while the renter will repay the government.
Renters will need to pay the difference if the second bond is higher – equally they will be refunded the difference if it is cheaper, provided there is no agreed claim on the bond.
The NSW government scheme has already seen $1m in bond transfers in Penrith, Parramatta and the Central Coast, where it was rolled out early.

It follows similar moves to make renting fairer in NSW, including a ban on no grounds evictions, a limit of one rent increase a year, enforcing fee-free ways to pay rent and making it easier for people to have pets.
NSW One Nation leader fronts rally opposing 'abortion to birth'

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy

The head of One Nation in New South Wales has fronted a rally opposing “abortion up to birth” ahead of an expected vote in the upper house on Libertarian member John Ruddick’s bill to ban “sex-selective abortions” during private member’s business today.

Mike Newman appeared alongside members of fringe parties outside the state’s parliament house on Tuesday evening, where he claimed One Nation wanted to “stop” abortion rights. Stumbling upon his words, he told the crowd:

double quotation markWe want to stop it. We want to make sure that same-sex-, sorry, abortion is stopped. We want to make sure that people have the right to life, and we will vote for you in favour of that.

Debate on Ruddick’s bill was adjourned in the June sitting week, and is expected to be decided via a conscience vote. Labor and opposition sources said the vote was expected to be close, or for support for Ruddick’s bill to fall slightly short.
The event follows another anti-abortion rally in June, attended by One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, where he piled pressure on Nationals MPs to vote on favour of the bill.

Some members were expected to be absent for today’s vote, including Shooters, Farmers and Fishers MLC Robert Borsak, who spoke in favour of the bill in June. A senior Liberal source said that without members including Borsak, there did not appear to be “any room or margin” which could deliver Ruddick’s bill.

Richard Marles was also asked about Aukus, and whether he was concerned about reports from the UK which indicated the Labour government was delaying its decision about begginning building the boats by two years to 2028.
He said there was “no change” on Australia’s end in terms of the UK’s position and rejected that they were “red flags”.

double quotation markThe ultimate number of submarines is not the key issue here, the key issue is the development of the design, the pace of that which is happening. The UK is on track to cut steel in respect of its first SSN Aukus submarine next year. It’s on track to have that submarine come off the production line in the UK in the late 2030s. That’s perfect timing in respect of what we’re doing … We are really comfortable with what is happening there.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, says he is “comforted” by a recent essay from the boss of artificial intelligence company Anthropic which warned his industry must slow the pace in developing AI systems.
Appearing on ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening, Marles was asked about Dario Amodei’s comments urging governments to press pause on the AI revolution.
He replied:

double quotation markI actually take comfort in Dario Amodei’s essay and the call he’s made … It’s firstly not about … stopping this all together but rather making sure that the development of the safeguards that are in place in respect of this technology is in front of the technological capability itself … The technology is being developed very quickly, and … from an Australian point of view, our focus is making sure that in seeing this as a revolutionary technology which can be doing so much good in Australia that, we do have in place … AI safeguards in Australia which make sure that this is a technology which is benefit Australians and not the other way around.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.
Jacqui Lambie has launched a fiery attack on Pauline Hanson, urging Australians not to support the “dangerous” and “delusional” One Nation leader. More coming up.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete competed while having diarrhea. Was she right to push through?
articles.summary: The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors…

image.caption: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in Hyrox Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval on Saturday in Beijing. Hyrox has been criticized online for not stopping Wietrzyk from competing despite having diarrhea. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.
Hyrox apologized after Australian Joanna Wietrzyk won Saturday's competition in Beijing
Popular indoor fitness competition Hyrox has said it has changed its protocols after allowing an Australian athlete to keep competing — and win — despite suffering from what appeared to be diarrhea.
"It's a biohazard, how they let the competition go on is beyond me," an observer wrote on Reddit.
"Think about how disgusting it is, especially when we use the exact same track," a race participant told the South China Morning Post.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.
"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

"Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not," co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement Monday.
"As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again," he added.

The Hyrox official rulebook already had some penalties in place for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited, but until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.
As some people have pointed out in the comments on Hyrox's Instagram apology, perhaps it's "unbelievable that this even needs a rule."
"That’s not a rule. That’s basic human decency," someone commented.
So, what happened?
Hyrox, a structured indoor activity divided into eight segments, each involving a one-kilometre run followed by a fitness exercise, attracts tens of thousands of participants to its biggest events.

The event was developed in 2017 by German entrepreneur Christian Toetzke and Moritz Fürste, who won field hockey gold medals for Germany in the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics. It's since become a global phenomenon, was accepted as a format in World Triathlon this year (under the name Hyathlon) and has its sights set on the Olympics.

items: 'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor
Botched Edmonton Marathon costs 13 runners chance at Boston Marathon

blocks.text: And Wietrzyk is the women's pro world record holder after her performance at the Warsaw Major in April. While she hasn't made an official statement about what happening in Beijing, several reports claim Wietrzyk was suffering from food poisoning.
A spectator at the event told the South China Morning Post that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.

Hyrox China, in a statement posted social media platform Weibo, said a competitor experienced a "sudden medical issue." The statement explained that organizers later disinfected contaminated areas, removed any contaminated equipment and replaced the carpet in the venue.
60-year-old teacher places 2nd at Hyrox world championship

As the TaiPei Times reports, Hyrox China did not apologize, but "admitted in an earlier statement to 'shortcomings' in the regulations which had prevented judges from intervening immediately during the competition."
Wietrzyk's coach, Chris Bayens, defended her in a statement posted to Instagram Sunday, urging people not to judge her "intent, clarity, or morality."
"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," Bayens wrote.
"What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time."
CBC News has reached out to Hyrox, Wietrzyk and her coach for comment, but not yet heard back.
Poop incidents are common

As many high-intensity athletes likely know, shit happens. Sometimes literally. There's even a term for it: runner's diarrhea, which Healthline describes as an inflammation of the colon caused by the intensity of workouts that can lead to frequent bowel movements.

According to a 2014 study, anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent of athletes report gastrointestinal problems. More recently, a 2025 literature review published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology concluded that high-intensity or prolonged exercise may contribute to symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

items: Olympic-bound sprinter trapped in toilet before race unlocks new bathroom fear in fellow runners
Canadian athletes fighting stomach illness at Paris Olympics

blocks.text: There are many well-documented and highly public cases where athletes have soiled themselves mid-competition. Just this past June, for instance, South African runner George Kusche won the Comrades Marathon with feces dripping down his legs.
Meanwhile, U.S. athlete Taylor Knibb won the 2024 T100 World Championship in Dubai, but made headlines for telling a cameraman, "I just shit myself. So can you not get my ass?"
Hyrox is coming to Ottawa and athletes are training at this 24/7 pop-up gym

In 2021, another U.S. athlete, Addi Zerrenner, went viral after soiling herself three times while running the California International Marathon, and told Business Insider, "I'm finally having the true marathon experience."
And U.K. runner Paula Radcliffe famously won the 2005 London Marathon after having to stop at 22-mile mark to defecate on the sidelines, calling it "an embarrassing necessity."
But, as many observers have noted, these incidents have all occurred outdoors.

Meanwhile, another Hyrox competitor, Malaysia's Zarif Zakaria, posted on Threads that he was recently disqualified from the Aug. 13 competition in Bangkok for using the bathroom — before the race. He claimed it's because it meant he had a late start.
"How come people can race while having diarrhea and not get DQ’d?" he posted Monday.
"Maybe it's time for me to retire from HYROX."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.
