articles.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
articles.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.

blocks.text: Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities
By
Reporting fromZaporizhzhia oblast
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."

Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.

As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.

blocks.caption: Map of Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control. Territories under Russian control are shaded pink, including Crimea, most of the occupied areas of Donetsk, large parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and a continuous belt of territory along the Sea of Azov connecting Crimea to e…

blocks.text: That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.

Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."

blocks.caption: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: BBC
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in

blocks.caption: "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in", Source: Igor Smelyansky, Source description: Head of Ukrposhta, Image: Igor Smelyansky stands in his blue Ukrposhta shirt and smiles at the camera. He has greying dark hair, and wears stubble with a smile

blocks.text: If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."

Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.

She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

blocks.text: Ukraine's post office provides a vital lifeline for people near the front, delivering pensions and medicine

One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."

Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"

But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.

She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

blocks.text: Kateryna Marynych has lost her home and her husband in this war - now, she's also lost her post office

The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.

For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.

Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

articles.title: ‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
articles.summary:
Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing

When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners…

blocks.text: When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.

However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.

After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.
Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.
Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.

blocks.caption: The first group of Afrikaners arrived in the US under Trump’s refugee programme in early May 2025. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.

The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.
On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.

“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.

It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.

While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.

“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”

blocks.caption: During a meeting on 21 May 2025, Donald Trump ambushed his South African counterpart, Cyril Ramaphosa, with printed-out news articles about a ‘white genocide’ in his country. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA

blocks.text: Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees Last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.

Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.

The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.
They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.

Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.

The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”

In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.

“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow
articles.summary:
Almost 3,500 people have died in outbreak and experts say more must be done to ensure Bundibugyo is under control

Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the…

blocks.text: Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.
For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.

Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola.

“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.

“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.
Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.

The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.

No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common Zaire Ebola virus.

blocks.caption: Children read an information poster about Ebola in Bunia, Ituri province, which is one of the areas of the DRC hardest hit by the outbreak.  Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters

blocks.text: According to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than 7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.

While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.
Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.

The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

He warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.

Early last month, Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but that containment and contact tracing were still not effective enough.

Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”

In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.
“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”

articles.title: Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes Emmy Awards history with double win
articles.summary: He becomes the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night at the prestigious TV ceremony.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Matthew Rhys was named best lead actor in a comedy and best lead actor in a limited series
ByIan Youngs and Steven McIntosh
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.
Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.
On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".
"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding "Diolch yn fawr iawn" - which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.

items: The winners and nominations in full
The red carpet in pictures

blocks.text: Other winners of the coveted US TV awards included Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Stephen Colbert, while there was an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a special humanitarian award for Michael J Fox.
Watch: Selena Gomez, Zendaya and other stars light up Emmys red carpet
Proud Rhys flies the flag
Rhys was named best lead actor in a limited series for The Beast In Me, then won best lead actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay.

A small number of actors, including Alan Alda, Sally Field, John Goodman, Elisabeth Moss and Ted Danson, have been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year, but Rhys is the first to score a double win.
Backstage, he said: "I'm from a small country, and I'm glad we get moments to kind of put our flag on the map and say, 'we punch higher than our weight sometimes'."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rhys attended the ceremony with his partner, US actress Keri Russell, who was also nominated for an Emmy

blocks.text: Rhys attended the ceremony with his partner, US actress Keri Russell, who was also nominated for an Emmy
The Beast In Me follows a grieving author, played by Claire Danes, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious new neighbour suspected of murder.

Rhys said it was a "real shock" to win the award, adding: "Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast, you are an intimidating scene partner, but I'm grateful for all this."

Later in the night, accepting the comedy actor prize for playing the mayor in Widow's Bay, he thanked the family, friends and colleagues who supported his career, including his parents who "kicked me on to the stage at a very early age".
A win for 'Lancashire lass'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kate O'Flynn thanked Widow's Bay producers for "trusting this Lancashire lass"

blocks.text: Kate O'Flynn thanked Widow's Bay producers for "trusting this Lancashire lass"

His Widow's Bay co-star Kate O'Flynn was among the other British winners, being named best supporting comedy actress for playing Patricia in the show about a fictional island beset by a centuries-old curse.
"I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow's Bay, in front and behind the camera," said O'Flynn, from Bury in Greater Manchester.
She added: "This is the role of a lifetime... Thank you for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia."
Smart and Janney equal Emmys record

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jean Smart and Allison Janney equalled the same Emmys record, minutes apart

blocks.text: Jean Smart and Allison Janney equalled the same Emmys record, minutes apart
Elsewhere, Jean Smart won best comedy actress for her role in the fifth and final series Hacks.
It is the fifth Emmy she has won for the Hollywood satire. "What a ride this has been," Smart reflected, and joked that the audience only gave her a standing ovation "because I'm old".
It was Smart's eighth Emmy win in total, and The Diplomat's Allison Janney also picked up the eighth Emmy of her career, triumphing in the category for best supporting actress in a drama series.
Smart and Janney have both now equalled the record for the most acting wins ever, shared with Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus.
Despite her past success, Janney was a surprise winner on Monday and said she was "genuinely shocked" to see off competition from four stars of hospital drama The Pitt, among others.

Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn won the first Emmy of her career for best lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus, the Apple TV show about a woman who discovers almost everyone else in the world has been taken over by a mysterious mind virus.
The Pitt scoops top prize

blocks.caption: Image caption, Noah Wyle has won best lead actor in a drama series for two consecutive years

blocks.text: Noah Wyle has won best lead actor in a drama series for two consecutive years
The Pitt won best drama, traditionally seen as the most prestigious award of the night.
And the show's leading star Noah Wyle also picked up the trophy for best lead actor in a drama series for the second year in a row.

"I'm a Hollywood kid. I was raised on a television, and movie theaters were my place of worship," Wyle told the audience. "This is all I've ever wanted to do and this is the only club I've ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me."
The former ER star praised all of his fellow nominees, but singled out veteran British star Sir Gary Oldman, who was nominated for Slow Horses.

Wyle said he was inspired by Sir Gary's performance as Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious in 1986 film Sid and Nancy, recalling how at the time he thought it was "the benchmark that I want to hit one day in my career".
Hero's welcome for Michael J Fox

blocks.caption: Image caption, Michael J Fox was nominated for his guest role in Shrinking as well as receiving the honorary humanitarian accolade

blocks.text: Michael J Fox was nominated for his guest role in Shrinking as well as receiving the honorary humanitarian accolade
Michael J Fox was given a standing ovation as he received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his campaigning for support for Parkinson's disease.

The Back to the Future star, 65, who founded the Michael J Fox Foundation in 2000, said: "When it starts getting tough, you show up, you help, and if you get a little joy while you're doing it, that's even better."
Appearing in a wheelchair, he told the ceremony he initially kept his condition secret after being diagnosed at the age of 29.

But he added: "Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease. So I set out to advocate for patients' needs and raise money, and to propel us towards a cure."
Dolly Parton tribute

blocks.caption: Image caption, Reba McEntire performed Dolly Parton's Appalachian Memories

blocks.text: Reba McEntire performed Dolly Parton's Appalachian Memories
Actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month.
Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.
"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy in 2021.
"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on Earth who will love you for ever and ever."
Earlier in the night, Field won best actress in a limited series or movie for Remarkably Smart Creatures, a Netflix film about an octopus who observes the staff in his aquarium.
Catherine O'Hara remembered

blocks.caption: Image caption, Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy shared their memories of Catherine O'Hara

blocks.text: Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy shared their memories of Catherine O'Hara

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to".
Referring to the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."
Noah Kahan then performed Bridge Over Troubled Water during the in memoriam segment, before Jamie Lee Curtis paid an emotional tribute to actor and director Rob Reiner.
Reiner, who died last December, received a posthumous Emmy last week for his guest appearance in The Bear.
Alan Cumming's 'beautiful treachery'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cumming won best reality host for The Traitors during a preliminary Emmys ceremony last week

blocks.text: Cumming won best reality host for The Traitors during a preliminary Emmys ceremony last week

In other award categories, Scottish TV presenter Alan Cumming accepted the best reality show prize for the US version of The Traitors, an honour he said would encourage the team to "do better and go bigger".
"It is so beautiful that a show about treachery and betrayal brings people together," he joked, as he also thanked his dog Lala, "the perfect co-host".
On an evening otherwise light on political messages, Cumming concluded his speech by encouraging US citizens to register to vote ahead of the midterm elections in November.
Stephen Colbert's swansong

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colbert won for his late-night talk show, which ended in May after being cancelled

blocks.text: Colbert won for his late-night talk show, which ended in May after being cancelled
Stephen Colbert won best variety series after presenting his final episode of The Late Show in May.

The presenter said nightly talk shows were a "fantastic incubator for young people to come in, work professionally, on a deadline, in collaboration, and that is the future of our business that we have to look after".
He added: "I want to say to the audience, thank you so much for watching, we hope you enjoyed the show, we had a great time doing it for you. That's it, thank you, and catch you on the flip."

articles.title: Nato jets shoot down drone violating Lithuania’s airspace
articles.summary:
The drone, which reportedly entered from Belarus, ⁠was shot down near Pratkunai village in central-southern Lithuania

Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was…

blocks.text: Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the ‌capital, Vilnius, and surrounding region, while Poland scrambled fighter jets less than a day after retrieving a suspected Russian drone adrift in its waters.

The Lithuania drone ⁠was shot down near the central-southern village of Pratkunai outside the city of Kaunas, said emergency authorities early on Tuesday. The drone came from neighbouring Belarus and was heading west, according to information from Lithuania’s crisis management centre that was reported by national radio LRT.

Gitanas Nauseda, the Lithuanian president, posted in the early hours of Tuesday: “A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by Nato fighter jets. With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region.”

Poland ⁠meanwhile activated its air force as ​a preventive ‌measure ‌amid Russian drone attacks ‌on Ukraine. On Monday, the Polish military recovered a suspected Russian drone from the sea ⁠on the Baltic coast ⁠in ​northern Poland.
On Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian foreign minister, Kestutis Budrys, thanked allies “whose presence helps protect our skies and strengthens our security”.
“This is best example of allied unity and resolve in action – sending a clear message that Nato stands vigilant, committed, and ready.”
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all Nato members on the Russian border – have repeatedly had drone incursions into their territories since Moscow began its war against Ukraine.

A Nato fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, the first interception of a foreign drone in the airspace of a Baltic state by Nato air police since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In Poland, the defence minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, said on Monday: “The military has located ⁠and recovered a drone from the Baltic Sea near the ​beach in Rusinowo, close ‌to Jaroslawiec.
“Preliminary inspection indicates that it is a Russian military ‌drone.”

A Polish armed forces spokesperson said the drone appeared to be a Gerbera – a cheap long-range aerial drone made of materials like plywood and foam. They are often used as decoys but can also carry explosives. It was recovered by a hydrographic vessel off the coast of the village of Rusinowo.
The Polish prime minister, ​Donald Tusk, has ​repeatedly warned that Nato countries ​should expect an increase in provocations from Moscow.

A ​Russian drone hit ‌a passenger ​train on ​Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, shortly after former the British prime minister, Boris Johnson, and other foreign diplomats had used the same line.

articles.title: AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act
articles.summary: With Trump opposed and Congress divided, new safety legislation on AI is unlikely to pass anytime soon despite mounting pressure.

blocks.text: When President Donald Trump responded to mounting calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) on Monday, he was unequivocal.

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on social media. He earlier argued that "the only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs" is a "strong and smart" president.

Trump's view, unsurprisingly, is not shared by senior Democrats in Congress. It is also opposed by leading figures in the AI sector, who have in recent days issued stark safety warnings and made the case for government regulation.
In the US, however, new safety legislation on AI is unlikely anytime soon.

Any bill would have to pass in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to become law. Trump's staunch opposition to new guardrails on AI means the Republican Party, which has a majority in both chambers, is unlikely to break from him and back restrictions or government controls.

And even if they did, whatever bill is passed would most likely require the president's signature to take effect. Trump's dismissal of the need for regulations on Monday effectively hit pause on any hope for executive action.
Over the weekend, Republican congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna suggested on X that "Congress SHOULD convene a special session" on the issue.

But it is highly unlikely the recess will be delayed or a special session convened in the coming days. Speaker Johnson, who on Monday faced a barrage of questions about AI from reporters in the halls of Congress, gave no sign he intended to move quickly this week.
When asked if the House would take action on AI concerns before breaking for the midterms, he replied: "This is a very complex issue."

He said Trump would hold a meeting at the White House soon with AI executives to discuss "the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety and what role, if any, the government has to play in that".
"We want to emphasise the necessity of [AI companies] providing safe products and self-regulating," Johnson said, before adding: "There is also a role potentially for Congress to play."
What that role could look like is unclear - and is a contested question among those in Congress.
While Democrats are pushing for more time to address AI safety, they are themselves divided on how best to regulate AI.
Even if the party were to win control of both chambers of Congress in November's elections, there are no guarantees of swift action as it would have to unite behind one proposal.

And there are numerous legislative proposals already on Capitol Hill that are designed to address AI safety, ranging from independent reviews, to a federal "kill switch", to a total moratorium on data centres proposed by Senator Bernie Sanders.
These diverging proposals point to a lack of consensus in Congress - but also an urgency among some lawmakers to take action.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune and his Democratic colleague Amy Klobuchar are working on a bill that would force some AI companies to submit to federal oversight.
"You don't want to stifle innovation," Thune said on Monday, "but I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated."
Some leading Republicans, including Speaker Johnson, have often referred to "self-regulation" when discussing government action and called on the companies to take responsibility for AI safety.

One of Trump's top AI advisers, David Sacks, told the BBC's US partner CBS News on Monday that some of the existential warnings by insiders had been overblown. "I think this is becoming a panic," he said.
"First and foremost, it is on them to make their products safe," Sacks said. "They should tell us how they should do that. If they can't do that, they should step aside for people who can do that."

"Why are you acting like this is something that you can't control?" he said, referring to Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei, who has called for a slowdown in development. "If you can't control it, then don't do it."
Some experts share the view that, in the short-term at least, it is up to the AI companies to regulate themselves responsibly.

"You might want an act of Congress, and I would love a congressionally mandated regime that requires safety and testing and bias testing," said Asad Ramzanali, the director of AI & Technology Policy at Vanderbilt University.
"But absent that action, the companies have autonomy."
Others have expressed scepticism at the recent flurry of warnings by AI staffers.
Trevor Traina, a tech executive who was a diplomat during Trump's first term, said: "I don't think the typical citizen has encountered anything scary or really problematic with AI."

"We're relying on the tweets of a half-dozen people who are all vying for perceived supremacy," he said. "The cynic in me thinks, 'Are they are really concerned, or are they trying to prove which model is the most awesome?'"

Alexandra Reeve Givens, who previously worked in government and now leads the US non-profit the Center for Democracy and Technology, said she did not think meaningful federal AI regulation would pass in the foreseeable future.

While the Trump administration has set up an entirely voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their models and tools for government assessment, Givens noted that the framework itself remains a secret.
"There's no clear standard to make sure that the approach is even grounded in the rule of law," she said.
Appeals from various groups to release the framework have so far gone ignored.
The White House approach, combined with a lack of political will and consensus, makes passing laws around AI difficult.
"There is no question that federal legislation is challenging in this climate, but Congress also has to grapple with which of the many types of AI risk need to be addressed," Givens said.
"It's not that AI is ungovernable, it's that each risk needs a tailored approach."

articles.title: Panama canal traffic to be cut again as drought from El Niño worsens
articles.summary:
Latest daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes

The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El…

blocks.text: The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.

The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.

From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.

In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.

Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.

The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.
The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.
If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.

In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.
El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year.

Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme.
The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia.
More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it.
Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.

articles.title: Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
articles.summary: The origin of the drone is currently unknown, but authorities say it likely entered Lithuania from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Russia.

blocks.text: Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.
Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.
Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.

Nausėda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Moscow has not commented on the incident.
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.
Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.
Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.
Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Mass nesting brings swarms of turtles to Mexican beach
articles.summary: Thousands of turtles arrived at La Escobilla beach in Oaxaca within 48 hours, sanctuary officials said.

blocks.text: Thousands of olive ridley turtles came to La Escobilla beach in Oaxaca, Mexico, to lay their eggs within 48 hours, according to sanctuary officials.
The natural phenomenon is known as "la arribada", meaning "the arrival", and sees hundreds of thousands of the reptiles swim ashore in southern Mexico.
This is the sixth wave of the creatures in the nesting season, which started in March.

articles.title: Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'
articles.summary: An Instagram post from the couple said two nights of their wedding festivities in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev.

blocks.text: Donald Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Trump, confirmed that their May wedding was paid for in part by an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

A post on her Instagram account - attributed to the couple - said that two nights of their three-day wedding festivities on a private island in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Putin.
The statement was released Monday after investigative journalism outlet ProPublica published a story detailing that Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars" for the celebration.
Donald Trump Jr., one of the US president's sons, is a private citizen, so it's not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national.

"Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," the couple said in the statement.

But ethics watchdog groups said it still presented the appearance of a conflict of interest for the president's son to accept lavish gifts from someone associated with a foreign head of state - even if he is not a US government employee.

"People don't just give hundreds of thousands of dollars to a random acquaintance without wanting something," said Jordan Libowitz, vice president of communications for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).
"You can see how [Putin] would enjoy all this press about how people in his circle are cozying up to people in the president's circle."

According to the ProPublica article, the couple was married on a private island in the Bahamas, then held a two-day celebration on a separate island that rents for approximately $100,000 per night. Kremlev also paid other costs for the party, including a roughly $70,000 fireworks display, the report found.

Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), an organization funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The Olympic Committee suspended the group in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.
Earlier this year Kremlev was part of a delegation that visited China with Putin. The Russian president also gave Kremlev the Order of Friendship, a top state honor, according to ProPublica.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship."
An ally of Trump Jr. referred the BBC to the Instagram statement.
In a statement to ProPublica, Kremlev's office said "Mr. Kremlev and Mr. Trump Jr have a friendly relationship." The statement said the men met a few years ago.

Kremlev attended part of the wedding, the outlet reported. Other attendees included one of the US president's daughters, Ivanka Trump, and her husband, Jared Kushner, who has worked for the US on diplomatic negotiations with Iran, Russia and in the Middle East.

The Trump campaign and family faced controversy for potential ties to Russia during the 2016 presidential election, resulting in a special counsel investigation. During the campaign Donald Trump Jr. brokered a meeting at Trump Tower with a Russian operative that was closely scrutinized during the probe.

Libowitz, of CREW, said either the president, who is a billionaire, or Trump Jr. -- who is worth $300 million, according to Forbes -- could have paid for the full wedding to avoid a conflict of interest.
"His father is worth billions he could have picked up the tab. Clearly they just didn't want to pay for it," Libowitz said. "They don't really care about the ethical ramifications."

articles.title: ‘Great’ or ‘alarming’ - Should AI be reined in?
articles.summary: The BBC asked people in Washington DC about the technology’s rapid development and whether it poses a threat to humanity, as some experts warn.

blocks.text: The rapid development of artificial intelligence and fears over the risks the technology poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over the weekend called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored.
The BBC spoke to people in Washington DC to learn how concerned they are over the technology and it's speedy development.
Video by Meiying Wu

articles.title: Legendary costume designer Bob Mackie dies aged 87
articles.summary: The "Sultan of Sequins" created iconic and dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John.

blocks.text: Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.
The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.
"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.
The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.
The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.

"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.
Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".
"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.
Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.

Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.

"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."

Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."
"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."
Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.

He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.

articles.title: EU seeks Arctic strategy amid growing power rivalry
articles.summary: Russia's aggression, Trump's threats against Greenland and the race for critical raw materials are pushing the Arctic to the top of Europe's agenda.

image.caption: Looking ahead: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders gathered in Finland to discuss the future of the ArcticImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia's war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention.
"There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition."
The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest."
A changing security environment in the High North

The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North.
"We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said.

The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and … uses its presence for hybrid activities every day."
Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials.

blocks.caption: European leaders learned about Finnish fighter jets during the Arctic summit as wellImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Confrontation replaces cooperation
"From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland.

For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe.

The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies.
Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities.

"But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW.
The United States as an additional stress factor

The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies.

"Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation."
Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkilä believes the region is increasingly divided.
"In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW.
He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights.
"Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkilä.
Inside NATO's Arctic operation preparing for a Russia crisis
Climate change is transforming the Arctic

At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova.
Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners.

"Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said.

He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change."
Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience'
At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience.
"We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said.

Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown.
